update_risk.title: Wrong clinical code assigned by the AI tool that reads notes
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-001. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-001
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads clinical notes assigns the wrong clinical code to what a clinician has written. This can happen when the AI misreads the meaning of the words used.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The AI tool assigns a wrong clinical code to a patient encounter. The clinician reviewing the record does not spot the error. The system then places the patient on the wrong clinical pathway based on that incorrect code.
update_risk.harm_description: If wrong clinical codes build up across many records, audit reports become inaccurate. Clinical teams may then focus quality improvement work in the wrong areas. Future patients may receive care based on misleading data.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the AI workflow keeps important clinical detail, such as whether a condition is confirmed or suspected, when it assigns a clinical code. This reduces the chance of a wrong code being chosen in the first place (DI-6A0B55A4). Second, the AI follows a structured set of rules when linking clinical ideas together, which limits the codes it can choose to those that make clinical sense (DI-3EA60D5A). Third, when a clinician reviews a coding decision, the screen shows exactly which words in the notes led the AI to choose that code. This helps the clinician spot and correct errors quickly (DI-4221A226). Fourth, the review screen also shows how often each code has been used historically for similar notes. This helps the clinician judge whether the AI choice looks unusual (DI-22F4E3CE). Fifth, before the AI tool is used in live care, it must achieve an accuracy score of at least 0.85 on a set of notes checked by a clinical expert. It cannot go live if it falls below this threshold (DI-12015DBC). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data on coding accuracy every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

update_risk.title: The AI tool that reads notes misses a clinically important finding
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-002. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-002
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes fails to spot a clinically important finding written in free text. This means the finding is not added to the coded record.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A symptom, diagnosis, or referral is written in the consultation notes. The AI tool that reads notes does not pick it up. The finding is left out of the coded record. When the system checks the patient's care pathway, the missing finding is not considered. A safety-net alert that should fire may not fire.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient's clinical record is incomplete. Their care pathway may appear shorter or simpler than it really is. A safety-net alert that should warn the clinician about a missed or delayed diagnosis may not appear. This could delay the patient receiving the right care.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, every time the AI tool that reads notes suggests a clinical code, a human reviewer must approve or reject it before it is saved to the audit record. This stops unchecked or missed findings from entering the final record without a clinician's decision (DI-4247C7E5). Second, when the AI tool pulls information from notes, it records how confident it is and where in the notes it found the finding. The reviewer can see exactly what the AI found and how sure it was (DI-31126C6C). Third, the AI tool's accuracy is tested against a set of examples checked by an expert before the system is used. It must reach a minimum accuracy score of 0.85. If it does not, the system is not released (DI-12015DBC). Fourth, the AI tool that decides if a finding is present, absent, or possible shows its reasoning on the coding review screen. The reviewer sees the evidence before approving any code (DI-375C7EB1). Fifth, confidence thresholds are set separately for different types of clinical finding. This means the system applies stricter checks where the clinical risk is higher (DI-F0B8A7B0). Sixth, if the main AI method cannot confidently identify a finding, a backup AI method is used and clearly labelled as a fallback. The reviewer can see which method produced the suggestion (DI-88C8BBCD). Seventh, when the system cannot reliably check a finding, it records a failed verdict and does not silently pass the case through. This prevents missed findings from going unnoticed (DI-9D967259). Eighth, every clinical statement in the record carries a link back to the original consultation note and the coded finding it came from. Reviewers and clinicians can trace any entry back to its source (DI-740BE510 and DI-B2512CB3). Ninth, the AI tool produces a structured summary for each patient that includes pathway stage and any safety-net alerts. This gives the reviewing clinician a clear overview even if individual findings were hard to extract (DI-30D9CC61). Tenth, safety-net alerts are only suppressed when a coded clinical response has been confirmed. This means an alert cannot be silently switched off because of a missed finding (DI-0E215ADE). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs, reviewer decisions, and alert firing rates every quarter to check these controls are working.

update_risk.title: The AI tool misreads context in clinical notes (for example, treating a denied symptom as present)
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible can get this wrong. For example, it may read 'no chest pain' and record chest pain as present. This means the patient's record holds an incorrect clinical finding.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The AI tool correctly spots a clinical term in the notes but wrongly decides what it means. A symptom the patient does not have may be recorded as present, or a real symptom may be missed. This pushes the patient into the wrong care pathway.
update_risk.harm_description: The wrong pathway classification could mean a patient receives care they do not need, or misses care they do need. Audit reports based on these records would also be inaccurate, making it harder to spot wider safety problems.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the AI workflow stores the exact words from the notes alongside every context decision, so a clinician can see why the AI reached its conclusion (DI-23822663). Second, every clinical statement in the record carries a clear link back to the original consultation and the clinical code it came from, giving clinicians a full audit trail (DI-740BE510). Third, before any results are used, the AI workflow must reach at least 85% accuracy against cases checked by an expert clinician; results that fall below this threshold are not released (DI-736B698B). Fourth, the AI workflow monitors its own accuracy over time; when accuracy drops, an alert is raised, the cause is recorded, and a full two-year history of alerts is kept and cannot be altered (DI-B1E0EE52). Fifth, when a clinician reviews a clinical code, the screen shows the context decision the AI made and the exact words it used to reach that decision, so errors can be spotted and corrected quickly (DI-375C7EB1). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

update_risk.title: The AI tool picks the wrong clinical code when several codes could match
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk | Workshop flag: Dedup Auditor - keep both but cross-link. R-055 is a high-severity subset of R-004.
update_risk.hazard_description: When a clinical term could match more than one clinical code, the AI tool that reads notes may pick the wrong one. For example, 'chest pain' could map to a cardiac cause or a musculoskeletal cause. The AI may choose the wrong option.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient's condition is linked to the wrong clinical code. This means the patient may be placed in the wrong clinical group. They could be incorrectly included in, or left out of, a care pathway or review list.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient may miss a review or follow-up they need. Alternatively, they may be flagged for a pathway that does not apply to them. Either way, their care could be delayed or misdirected.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the AI workflow uses a fixed set of episode status labels — confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive — to record how confident it is about each code match. This reduces the chance of a wrong code being treated as certain (DI-37DDAADE). The clinical safety team checks this labelling is applied consistently at each software release. Second, where a clinical term could overlap with more than one code, the AI workflow classifies all possible matches at the same time rather than forcing a single choice. This preserves ambiguity for a clinician to review (DI-DC61F5B6). The clinical safety team audits a sample of overlapping matches each quarter. Third, the AI tool that reads notes keeps clinical detail — such as 'possible', 'ruled out', or 'family history of' — when pulling information from notes. This extra detail helps the AI pick the most specific correct code (DI-6A0B55A4). Clinicians review a sample of these extractions monthly. Fourth, the AI workflow builds each episode from a consistent set of related encounters using fixed rules, so the same clinical information always produces the same code (DI-FF9C74E2). The technical team runs automated checks on this at every release. Fifth, the system highlights the exact words in the original note that led to each code choice. A reviewing clinician can see the source text and correct any wrong match before it affects the patient record (DI-E81545BE). The clinical safety committee reviews audit findings from all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: A reviewer approves a wrong clinical code that then influences future coding suggestions
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: A clinician reviewing the AI tool's suggested clinical codes approves one that is wrong. The system saves this wrong code as a preferred match for that piece of text. The AI tool then uses it to nudge future coding suggestions whenever the same wording appears in notes.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A reviewer approves a wrong clinical code for a phrase in a patient's notes. The system saves this as a learned preference. The next time the AI tool reads the same phrase in any patient's notes, it gives that wrong code a higher ranking in its suggestions. Future clinicians see the wrong code near the top of the list.
update_risk.harm_description: Future patients whose notes contain the same phrase may be coded incorrectly if a clinician accepts the boosted wrong suggestion without checking. This could affect their care pathway or records. The wrong code is a suggestion only, not an automatic entry, so a clinician still has to choose it.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, before the system saves any approved code back into the shared code library, it runs an automatic check to confirm the code is valid and consistent with related codes already stored. This check runs every time a reviewer approves a code (DI-1B8AC856). Second, the system stores the exact sentence or phrase from the notes alongside every saved code. Reviewers and the safety team can read this context to spot whether a saved code makes sense for the words it was matched to. This is available at all times (DI-23822663). Third, the shared code library is held in a completely separate database from patient records. A problem in one cannot directly corrupt the other. This separation is in place at all times (DI-84F44836). Fourth, when a reviewer selects a code to approve, the system highlights the exact words in the original note that the AI tool used to make its suggestion. This helps the reviewer check the match is correct before approving it (DI-E81545BE). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of approved codes and any reported mismatches every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

update_risk.title: Reviewers stop checking AI suggestions carefully over time
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: Clinicians reviewing AI suggestions may begin to trust them too much. Over time, they may stop checking each suggestion carefully. This is called automation bias.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A reviewer routinely approves AI coding suggestions without reading them properly. Errors in the AI suggestions pass through the review step unnoticed. The human review step no longer catches mistakes.
update_risk.harm_description: The main safety check — a clinician reviewing each AI suggestion — stops working as intended. Incorrect clinical codes enter the final audit data without being caught. This could lead to patients being wrongly included in or excluded from clinical audits, affecting the care they receive.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, every AI coding suggestion must receive an individual decision from a reviewer before it can enter the final audit data. No suggestion is approved automatically. The reviewer must actively accept or reject each one (DI-4247C7E5). Second, the system records how reviewers are engaging with suggestions. A clinical safety officer has a monitoring view that highlights signs of automation bias, such as very fast approval rates. The clinical safety officer checks this regularly (DI-22D862B0). Third, the system blocks audit reports from using any episode classification that has not been through human review. Unreviewed suggestions cannot reach the final data (DI-BD696225). Fourth, the system blocks any follow-on actions from guideline alerts that have not been reviewed by a clinician. This prevents unreviewed AI output from affecting patient pathways (DI-7913344A). The clinical safety committee reviews these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: A whole clinical area is coded wrongly, hiding problems in patient care pathways
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: gap. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes, or the way clinical codes are set up, causes every record in one clinical area to be coded in the same wrong way. For example, all referrals or all treatments in that area carry the wrong code. Because the error is consistent, it is hard to spot when reviewing individual patient records.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: Every encounter in a clinical area carries the same coding error. No single case looks obviously wrong. Routine checks on individual records do not flag the problem. The error builds up silently across the whole patient population.
update_risk.harm_description: When all records in a clinical area are coded wrongly in the same way, audit results look normal even when real problems exist. Clinicians and managers draw incorrect conclusions about the quality of care. Improvement efforts are aimed at the wrong areas. Patients who need changes to their care pathway do not receive them.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Five controls reduce this risk. First, before the AI workflow goes live, a dry-run check tests the full setup against a sample dataset to catch systematic coding errors early. The technical team runs this check every time the configuration changes (DI-ACB587DD). Second, completeness and suppression thresholds are set at programme level so that unusually low or high coding rates in any clinical area trigger an alert. The programme team reviews these thresholds at each release (DI-0D7DCC52). Third, population pathway dashboards show coding patterns for each clinical area alongside national benchmarks. Clinicians and the programme team review these dashboards monthly to spot any area where local figures diverge from expected national patterns (DI-BA2C8F3E). Fourth, when a coding error is found, a structured correction review checks all related codes and the rules the AI follows to make sure the fix does not introduce new errors elsewhere. The clinical informatics team carries out this review before any correction is applied (DI-1B8AC856). Fifth, the audit programme is configured using real data patterns so that checks are targeted at areas where systematic errors are most likely. The clinical safety team reviews the audit configuration at least quarterly (DI-CD931485). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all five controls are working at each quarterly meeting.

update_risk.title: Patient details accidentally saved into the clinical codes database
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: A software fault or developer mistake causes the system to save patient-identifiable details into the clinical codes database. This database holds the standard clinical codes used across the system, not individual patient records.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: Patient details end up in the clinical codes database. That database has wider access than the patient records database. Staff or system components that should not see patient details may be able to view them.
update_risk.harm_description: A patient's personal or clinical details are seen by people who should not have access. This breaches patient confidentiality and breaks UK GDPR and NHS information governance rules.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: IG/Security (GDPR + DCB0129).
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The patient records database and the clinical codes database are kept on completely separate systems so data cannot accidentally cross between them. The technical team maintains this separation at all times (DI-84F44836). Each tenant using the system gets their own dedicated patient database, which limits how far any accidental data leak can spread. The technical team sets this up automatically for every new tenant (DI-AF5A1668). Before any software change goes live, the team tests it in a safe practice environment using dummy patient data. Faults are deliberately triggered to check the separation holds. The technical team runs these tests before every release (DI-B8674FBF). A review process checks any corrections made to clinical codes to make sure no patient details have been mixed in. The clinical informatics team runs this check as part of every coding update (DI-1B8AC856). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all these controls are working every quarter.

update_risk.title: Patient-identifying details not removed from clinical notes before the AI tool reads them
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The step that removes patient-identifying details from clinical notes can fail. When it fails, names, NHS numbers, or other personal details stay in the text. The AI tool then processes notes that still contain this information.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A reviewer sees or a system log stores clinical notes that still contain a patient's name, NHS number, or other personal details. People who are not authorised to see that information may be able to access it.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient's confidential information is seen by people who should not see it. This breaks patient confidentiality and breaches UK GDPR.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: IG/Security (GDPR + DCB0129).
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: An audit trail system component records every time clinical notes are accessed or processed, without exposing the full patient record to unauthorised users. The clinical safety team reviews these audit records regularly to check whether any personal details have passed through incorrectly (DI-09E26C1D). The AI workflow stores a record of where each piece of information came from alongside the result it produced. This means reviewers and the safety team can trace exactly which notes were used and check whether personal details were present (DI-23822663). The system shows a confidence level next to every result the AI produces. A low confidence score prompts a reviewer to look more closely at the underlying notes, which may reveal that personal details were not removed (DI-DA7584D8). Results shown to reviewers are written in plain language rather than raw coded output. This makes it easier for a clinician to spot if personal details have been included in what is displayed (DI-66F1B177). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and reviewer feedback every quarter to confirm these controls are working. Additional controls are being identified, as the current linked design inputs do not include a direct technical control that prevents the de-identification step from failing in the first place.

update_risk.title: AI tool produces wrong clinical information from patient notes
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: gap. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes has not been trained well enough, or its accuracy has fallen over time. It starts identifying the wrong clinical information from patient records.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The AI tool that reads notes produces the same type of error repeatedly across a group of patient records. Nobody spots the problem before the tool is used in live clinical work. As a result, audit data drawn from those records is wrong for every patient affected.
update_risk.harm_description: Widespread errors in audit data could mean patients with a particular condition or medicine are missed or wrongly included in clinical reviews. This could delay care or trigger unnecessary clinical action across a large group of patients.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool records a confidence score and a full history of where each piece of clinical information came from. This lets reviewers trace and check any result the tool produces (DI-31126C6C). Second, the AI tool follows a fixed set of clinical rules when linking pieces of information together. This limits the types of error it can make (DI-3EA60D5A). Third, the audit programme is set up and tested using real patient data before any results go live. This catches systematic errors early, before they affect patients (DI-CD931485). Fourth, error categories can be updated at any time without stopping the system. The team responsible for the tool reviews and updates these categories whenever a new type of error is found (DI-770FD74A). Fifth, a versioned list of known errors is kept, with three clear categories and a defined fix path for each. The development team uses this list to resolve errors in a structured way (DI-990C0AFA). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: Patient notes sometimes contain text that the AI mistakes for instructions. This can make the AI behave in unexpected ways instead of reading the notes normally.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: When the AI reads a patient's free-text notes, it may treat certain phrases as commands. This can cause it to assign wrong clinical codes, miss important clinical findings, or behave unpredictably.
update_risk.harm_description: If wrong clinical codes are saved to the patient record, the patient's problem may be recorded incorrectly. This could affect future care decisions. The risk is low because a clinician checks all AI output before it is saved.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: IG/Security (GDPR + DCB0129).
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the AI workflow only uses structured, bounded facts when deciding the clinical meaning of a finding. This stops free-text phrases from changing how the AI interprets clinical information. The development team built this in by design and it runs automatically on every case (DI-69C29EEF). Second, a coding correction review checks that all clinical codes are valid and consistent before they are saved. This is carried out by the system automatically and flagged for clinician review where needed (DI-1B8AC856). Third, role-based access controls mean only authorised clinicians can review and approve AI output before it is saved to the patient record. This is enforced by the system on every action (DI-E83828A9). Fourth, the AI uses a precise position-tracking method to make sure each finding it pulls from the notes is matched exactly to the right piece of text. This reduces the chance of a finding being misread or misplaced (DI-A0C90595). Fifth, the AI preserves clinical qualifiers such as whether a condition is current, past, or possible, so that clinical codes remain as specific and accurate as possible (DI-6A0B55A4). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and any flagged cases every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system checks that all links between steps in the AI workflow stay intact from start to finish. This means a gap or break in the chain is detected before it can cause an incomplete record (DI-08DE2CF3). The clinical safety team reviews these checks at each software release. Second, before any new workflow setup goes live, the team runs a test pass to confirm the configuration works correctly end to end. This dry run is carried out by the technical team before every activation (DI-ACB587DD). Third, the system shows the results of each completed step as soon as that step finishes, even if the overall job has not yet ended. This means a clinician or reviewer can see which parts of the record are ready and which are not (DI-CB07829F). Fourth, the system is designed to complete a full single-patient workflow within ten seconds for most patients. This limits the window during which a record could be in an incomplete state (DI-620FE631). Fifth, any updates to clinical guidelines go through independent checks before they enter the workflow, reducing the chance that a faulty update triggers a failure mid-run (DI-F3EFEA88). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and re-run rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

update_risk.hazardous_situation: The AI tool reads notes less accurately after an update. It misses or misreads clinical terms across all patient records it processes. No alert is raised. The errors build up silently in the audit data before anyone detects the problem.
update_risk.harm_description: Patient records and audit data contain systematic errors. Clinicians or audit teams may act on incomplete or wrong information. This could lead to patients missing follow-up care or being placed on the wrong clinical pathway.

update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system records a confidence score and full source details every time the AI tool pulls a clinical term from a note. This means each result can be traced back to its origin and checked (DI-31126C6C). The clinical safety team reviews these records as part of routine quality checks. Second, the system continuously monitors coding quality and sends an alert if accuracy drops (DI-1126FFD1). The safety team reviews these alerts as they arise. If accuracy falls below the agreed level, the system halts and rolls back to the previous version without manual intervention (DI-7D710C52). update_risk.title: An update to the AI reading tool changes how it searches past encounters, making results less accurate
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: gap. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that searches past encounters uses a scoring method to find relevant records. If the AI tool is updated, the stored scores from before the update no longer match the new version. This means the search may return the wrong encounters or miss important ones.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: After an update to the AI tool, the system searches past encounters using mismatched scores. It may return irrelevant encounters and miss ones that matter. A clinician reviewing the shortlist could overlook a relevant past encounter when making a clinical decision.
update_risk.harm_description: A clinician may not see a relevant past encounter. This could lead to an incomplete picture of the patient's history. Any harm is likely to be minor, as other information sources remain available.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the system uses three different ways to search past encounters: keyword search, full-text search, and AI-based scoring. If the AI-based scoring is unreliable, the other two methods still return results. This means a single update cannot disable all search methods at once (DI-143F69EB). The clinical safety team reviews this design at each major update. Second, before any update goes live, the system must correctly find at least 95 in every 100 relevant encounters when tested against a set of encounters checked by an expert clinician. If it fails this test, the update is blocked (DI-10BB41E9). The technical team runs this test before every release. Third, the system stores accuracy figures for every version of the AI tool in a central log. The clinical safety team can compare figures before and after an update to spot any drop in performance (DI-CE0A08E5). This log is reviewed at each release and at quarterly safety meetings. Fourth, when a keyword search returns a strong match, the system uses that result directly and does not rely on AI-based scoring at all. This protects against poor AI scoring for clearly relevant encounters (DI-7A7BFA0C). This behaviour is tested as part of every release check. The clinical safety committee reviews all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: A routine clinical coding update breaks how the AI tool matches terms to clinical codes
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The UK clinical coding system (SNOMED CT) is updated several times a year. Each update can add new codes, retire old ones, or change how codes relate to each other. The AI tool that reads notes and assigns clinical codes may not handle these changes automatically.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: After a coding update, the AI tool may assign the wrong clinical code, fail to assign any code, or use a code that has been retired. This can happen silently, without any alert to the clinician. The error may affect many patients before it is noticed.
update_risk.harm_description: Patient records may carry incorrect clinical codes for a period of time. This could affect how patients are identified for recalls, audits, or care pathways. The risk is minor because a clinician reviews the record before any clinical decision is made.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, when a new coding update is released, the system automatically compares the new codes against the ones it currently uses and pauses any affected coding until a review is done. The technical team runs this check with every scheduled coding release (DI-B193C816). Second, the AI tool is designed to handle cases where two or more codes overlap or compete, reducing the chance of a wrong match after an update. The technical team maintains this as part of the AI workflow (DI-DC61F5B6). Third, before any updated coding rules go live, the AI tool must achieve a minimum accuracy score on a set of records checked by a clinical expert. The clinical safety team approves the results before release (DI-12015DBC). Fourth, when a coding correction is made, the system checks that all related codes and updated coding rules are consistent before saving changes back into the patient record. The technical team carries out this check at each release (DI-1B8AC856). Fifth, the AI tool that reads notes preserves important clinical detail, such as whether a condition is confirmed, suspected, or ruled out, so that the correct specific code is chosen even after an update changes code relationships. The technical team maintains this as part of the AI workflow (DI-6A0B55A4). The clinical safety committee reviews audit reports of coding accuracy after each SNOMED CT release to confirm all controls are working.

update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls are in place to reduce this risk. First, the system enforces strict rules about which versions of third-party components are allowed to run, blocking outdated or unsafe versions automatically (DI-F1A768AE). Second, a review process checks that all third-party components and clinical codes used in the AI workflow are valid and up to date (DI-1B8AC856). Fourth, a dedicated system component records a full audit trail of all activity, giving the safety team a way to investigate any suspicious access without exposing patient records directly (DI-09E26C1D). The safety team can query this audit trail at any time and must review it at least monthly. The clinical safety committee reviews all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.hazardous_situation: The wrong milestone date causes the system to calculate pathway waiting times incorrectly. It may show a breach of national waiting time targets that did not happen, or hide a real breach that did happen.
update_risk.harm_description: Clinicians and managers see inaccurate waiting time figures for groups of patients. Real performance problems may go unnoticed. Quality improvement effort may be directed at the wrong areas. Patients who have waited too long may not be identified and helped.

Third, the system applies quality checks before promoting any new version of the AI model that detects milestones. Only models that meet the required accuracy threshold are used in live calculations (DI-80BD2F86). The clinical safety committee reviews model promotion decisions each quarter. Clinicians and managers review these dashboards monthly. The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: gap. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The safety-net system does not spot patients who have reported possible cancer symptoms but have not been referred or investigated. The system misses the gap in their care.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient reports symptoms that could indicate cancer. No referral or investigation is arranged. The safety-net system does not raise an alert. No one follows up. The chance to catch the cancer early is lost.
update_risk.harm_description: Without a safety-net alert, the patient's lack of follow-up goes unnoticed. Their cancer may be diagnosed later than it should be. At a practice level, audit data is wrong and the team cannot see or fix the gap in care.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)

update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The system uses a configurable follow-up time window. If a patient with possible cancer symptoms has no recorded response within that window, the system adds them to a worklist for review by the clinical team. The team checks this worklist regularly (DI-4C73DC01). When a clinician records a confirmed clinical response using the correct clinical code, the system automatically removes the alert from the worklist. This stops unnecessary alerts for patients who have already been managed (DI-0E215ADE). The worklist can be filtered by how serious the finding is, how many days it has been outstanding, and which group of patients it covers. This helps the clinical team prioritise the most urgent cases (DI-520A8674). The audit programme can be updated to reflect new clinical priorities without needing a software deployment. This means the safety team can act quickly if a gap in care is identified (DI-CD931485). Every action taken on a safety-net alert is saved permanently with the clinician's name and the date and time it was recorded. This creates a clear record that can be reviewed at any time (DI-B46AD5CE). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

update_risk.title: Guideline compliance checker gives wrong alerts about care quality
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The compliance checker uses rules to decide whether a patient's care followed clinical guidelines. Sometimes it gets this wrong. It may flag care as a problem when it was fine, or miss care that genuinely fell short of guidelines.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: When the checker wrongly flags good care as a problem, clinical audit teams waste time investigating cases that need no action. This erodes trust in the tool. When the checker misses genuine problems, real gaps in patient care go uninvestigated and unresolved.
update_risk.harm_description: Missed problems mean genuine quality issues stay hidden. Patients may continue to receive care that falls short of guidelines without anyone noticing. Wrong alerts waste audit resource and make clinicians less likely to act on future alerts, including real ones.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system automatically checks each coded patient encounter against guideline rules and records a clear pass or fail result for every episode. The audit team can review these results at any time (DI-2AFF691F). Second, the rules engine lets the clinical team configure each rule and stores a pass, fail, or needs-action result alongside a suggested next step for every episode. This means no result is lost and every gap has a clear recommended action (DI-FC80B65A). Third, all patient record data enters and leaves the system through a single, standardised system component that follows an agreed data format. This reduces the risk of data being lost or misread before the rules are applied (DI-1795254D). Fourth, when a clinician reviews a flagged case and decides the deviation was clinically justified, they can record their reason without blocking their workflow. The system logs this rationale and shows which other patients in the same group were flagged for the same reason. This creates an auditable record of every decision (DI-6079EC71). Fifth, the AI tool that reads notes produces a structured summary for each patient, drawing on coded encounters, where the patient is in their care pathway, and any safety alerts. Clinicians can use this summary to quickly sense-check whether an alert looks right before acting on it (DI-30D9CC61). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs, alert accuracy rates, and clinician feedback every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: Wrong setup of an audit programme causes the AI workflow to process patient data incorrectly
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-068 FMEA-075. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-068 FMEA-075
update_risk.hazard_description: An administrator sets up an audit programme with wrong settings. This could include wrong patient groups, wrong clinical milestones, or wrong guideline rules.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: Because the programme is set up incorrectly, the AI workflow consistently looks at the wrong patients or applies the wrong clinical rules. It may count the wrong appointments, measure time between the wrong events, or flag the wrong patients as meeting or missing a guideline.
update_risk.harm_description: The audit produces wrong results for the affected programme. Clinicians and managers act on those wrong results. Quality improvement effort is directed at the wrong areas, and real problems in patient care may be missed.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, before any new programme setup goes live, the system runs a dry-run check to test whether the settings produce sensible results. The administrator reviews the output before the programme is activated (DI-ACB587DD). Second, all programme setup must be done through the system's own screen-based interface. If a test-mode check fails, the system blocks the administrator from moving the programme to live use without a deliberate override step (DI-F2C18D2E). Third, programme settings such as patient groups and clinical criteria can be changed directly in the system without needing a software release. This means errors can be corrected quickly by the administrator as soon as they are spotted (DI-CD931485). Fourth, when settings are updated, the changes take effect automatically at the next scheduled run without any system restart. This reduces the window in which wrong settings could affect results (DI-702F4583). Fifth, the guideline rules applied to each programme can be updated directly in the system by the administrator without a software release, allowing fast correction if a rule is found to be wrong (DI-AA8014F9). Sixth, the system automatically checks whether patient encounters carry the correct clinical codes before applying guideline rules. This catches cases where wrong codes would cause a patient to be incorrectly included or excluded (DI-2AFF691F). Seventh, the thresholds that decide whether an audit result is flagged as complete or suppressed are set at programme level and can be reviewed and adjusted by the administrator without a software release (DI-0D7DCC52). The clinical safety committee reviews audit outputs and configuration logs every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: The AI codes clinical information automatically, with no clinician check before saving
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: escalate_class_C. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: When the system runs in automatic mode, it assigns clinical codes to information found in patient notes. No clinician reviews or approves each coding decision before the code is saved to the patient record.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The AI reads clinical notes, identifies conditions and findings, and assigns clinical codes automatically. If the AI misreads the notes, picks the wrong code, or applies the wrong rules, an incorrect code is saved directly to the patient record. No clinician sees the decision before it is saved, so the error is not caught at the point it is made.
update_risk.harm_description: If the AI saves wrong clinical codes across many patient records before anyone notices, the data used for clinical audit and quality improvement becomes unreliable. Clinicians and managers making decisions based on that data may focus effort in the wrong areas, missing real problems or acting on false ones.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, a human-review gate stops any AI-generated clinical code from being saved to the patient record until a clinician has reviewed and approved it. This control applies in all modes where patient data could be affected. The clinical safety team checks this gate is active and working at every deployment (DI-604767B1). Second, when a clinician corrects a code, the system checks that the replacement code is valid, current, and consistent with related information already in the record. This check runs automatically every time a correction is made (DI-1B8AC856). Third, the AI preserves important clinical detail, such as whether a condition is current, historical, or suspected, when it reads notes and assigns codes. This reduces the chance of a code being saved with the wrong meaning. The AI workflow applies this rule on every note it processes (DI-6A0B55A4). Fourth, before any replacement code is accepted during a correction, the system confirms the code is current and has not been retired or replaced in the clinical coding system. This check runs automatically at the point of correction (DI-26CBDB16). Fifth, the AI follows a defined set of rules when identifying clinical relationships in notes, such as linking a medicine to the condition it treats. This reduces the chance of incorrect associations being coded. The rules are applied by the AI on every note it processes (DI-3EA60D5A). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

update_risk.title: A rule set too broadly stops a clinical term from being coded at all
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: A reviewer creates a rule that tells the AI workflow to ignore a clinical term everywhere in the notes. The rule should only apply in specific situations, such as when a patient is awaiting an appointment or when the term is used hypothetically. Because no limiting phrase is added, the rule removes the term from coding in every situation, including when it is genuinely present.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The rule silently removes all future mentions of the term before any clinician sees them. The term simply stops appearing in the review queue. No one is alerted. The gap in coding is invisible because there is nothing missing to notice.
update_risk.harm_description: A clinical condition such as hypertension (high blood pressure), diabetes review, or a biopsy result is consistently not coded across many patients. Audit figures show artificially low numbers of cases. Decisions about service planning and quality improvement are based on this incomplete data. Future patients may receive the wrong level of care as a result.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce the chance of this harm reaching patients. First, the AI tool that reads notes and the AI tool that decides whether something is present, absent, or possible are compared automatically after every processing run. If their results disagree for a given clinical term, the system flags the difference for review by the clinical informatics team (DI-F298AE65). Second, the system flags any clinical term it is not confident about, and it also flags when two coding decisions within the same patient episode contradict each other. A clinician reviewer checks these flags daily (DI-C7A810AA). Third, the AI workflow tracks how often each type of clinical term is coded over time. If the coding rate for any term drops below a set threshold, the system raises an alert to the clinical safety team. The safety team reviews these drift reports at least weekly (DI-37315D03). Fourth, all rules that control how the AI codes terms are held in a monitored registry under clinical change control. Any change to a rule must be approved before it goes live, and the full context of any alert is recorded. The clinical safety officer oversees this process and reviews the registry monthly (DI-ED3A89F5). All corrections made by reviewers in the unified review queue are stored as structured examples to improve future AI behaviour (DI-890BE989). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all four controls are working every quarter.

update_risk.title: Clinician makes an accidental or missed action in the coding review screen due to unclear warnings, hidden errors, or access barriers
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-006. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-006
update_risk.hazard_description: The coding review screen lets clinicians remove clinical codes, dismiss suggestions, or reset all work with a single click. There is no confirmation step before these actions take effect. When the system fails to load data, the screen looks the same as when there is genuinely nothing to review. Some clinicians using a keyboard may trigger actions by accident.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician clicks Remove, Dismiss, Create ignore rule, or Reset all without meaning to. The action happens immediately and is hard to undo. Separately, the system fails silently: the review queue appears empty, but this is because the system has not loaded properly, not because there is nothing to review. A clinician using only a keyboard may press a shortcut key by accident and reject a suggestion without intending to.
update_risk.harm_description: A correct clinical code may be deleted by accident. A broad ignore rule may be created, causing the system to suppress correct codes in future. Clinicians may skip the review queue believing it is empty, when in fact the system has failed to load outstanding work. Any of these errors could lead to clinical codes being missed or removed from patient records, distorting the clinical picture and audit data, and potentially affecting patient care decisions.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA).
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Role-based access control limits which clinicians can take destructive actions such as removing codes or creating ignore rules. Only authorised users can finalise or change AI suggestions. The system enforces this automatically on every action (DI-E83828A9). When a clinician corrects a suggestion, the system resets the confirmation step and requires the clinician to actively re-confirm before the change is saved. This stops accidental single-click changes from taking effect without a second check (DI-5ADEC3D1). A one-click option lets the clinician re-queue those records immediately, so a failed load is never mistaken for an empty queue (DI-69CE20C1). When a system component returns an error, the system records a structured error code rather than showing a blank screen. This means failures can be detected and investigated rather than going unnoticed (DI-6654FB0E). All review actions are recorded in a full audit trail. The safety team can check this trail to see whether accidental actions have occurred and whether failed loads were detected and resolved (DI-09E26C1D). The review screen shows how often a clinical code has been used historically. This gives the clinician a prompt to pause before removing an unusual or infrequent code, reducing the chance of accidental deletion (DI-22F4E3CE). The clinical safety committee reviews audit trail reports and failed-encounter logs every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.hazardous_situation: A lab result line is processed by the AI workflow. The AI tool decides the number means the patient has a specific disease. In fully automated mode, it is saved directly into the patient record without a clinician checking it first.

The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of coding suggestions and corrections every quarter to check these controls are working.

update_risk.title: Hidden instructions in patient notes cause the AI tool to give wrong clinical codes
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-012. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-012
update_risk.hazard_description: Patient notes sometimes contain text that looks like instructions to an AI tool. For example, someone might type phrases such as 'ignore all previous instructions' into a free-text field. When the AI tool reads these notes without checking for such phrases first, it may follow those hidden instructions instead of doing its coding task.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The AI tool reads raw patient encounter notes to check diagnoses and suggest clinical codes. If a malicious person adds hidden instruction phrases to a patient record, or if the GP system sends notes that already contain such phrases, those phrases reach the AI tool unfiltered. The AI tool may then return a wrong verdict on a diagnosis, or reveal information about how the system works internally.
update_risk.harm_description: The AI tool may wrongly mark an active diagnosis as uncertain, or wrongly confirm a diagnosis that is not present. update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: IG/Security (GDPR + DCB0129).
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the AI workflow replaces all patient-identifying details with neutral placeholders before any notes reach the AI tool. This is done automatically by the system every time notes are processed, with no way to bypass it (DI-F66A7239, DI-250F32EC). This reduces the risk that harmful phrases are linked to real patient data. Second, if the AI tool fails to return a valid verdict for any reason, the system automatically records a GATE_FAILED result and stops the coding process. This fail-closed design is built into the system and runs on every single coding attempt (DI-9D967259). Third, each coding decision is logged with a full record of what the AI tool did and why. Reviewers can see which part of the notes the AI tool used to reach its verdict. The clinical safety team checks these logs to spot any unusual or unexpected results (DI-09E26C1D, DI-E81545BE). Fourth, patient notes and clinical reference data are held in completely separate databases, so a compromised note cannot affect the coding reference data (DI-84F44836). Fifth, all data passing between system components is encrypted so it cannot be read or altered in transit (DI-155BB31E). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and system performance every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: An admin user creates harmful clinical rules that cause the AI tool to wrongly mark conditions as absent or suppress them entirely
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-012. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-012
update_risk.hazard_description: Users with admin access can create and change the rules that the AI tool follows when deciding whether a condition is present, absent, or possible in a patient's notes. They can also change rules that remove or relabel conditions after the AI has read the notes. An admin who makes a mistake, or acts with harmful intent, could create rules that are far too broad. This would cause the AI tool to wrongly handle every patient record processed after that point.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: Scenario one: an admin creates a rule linking a very common phrase in clinical notes to a setting that marks all nearby conditions as absent. Every future patient record containing that phrase has its conditions silently removed before a clinician sees them. Scenario two: an admin creates a badly formed text pattern that causes the AI workflow to lock up and stop processing records, blocking all coding work.
update_risk.harm_description: In scenario one, conditions that are genuinely present in patient records are never coded. This distorts disease prevalence data and quality-of-care audit results for every patient processed after the harmful rule is created. Clinicians and commissioners make decisions based on incomplete information. In scenario two, the AI workflow stops working entirely. No records are coded until the fault is found and fixed, causing delays to care pathway decisions that depend on coded data.

The guidance rule review queue requires a clinician to make an active decision before any rule change takes effect, and every change is linked to the records it affects (DI-F94EB13F). update_risk.title: Patient information sent to external AI services without confirmed data agreements
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-089. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-089
update_risk.hazard_description: The system uses two AI services at the same time to check clinical notes. When the two services disagree, a third AI service is asked to decide. Each of these calls sends text from the patient's GP record to an external cloud service. This means patient-identifiable information may be sent to up to three external services for a single piece of clinical information.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The system tries to remove patient-identifiable information before sending notes to the AI services. However, there are known gaps in this process: some unusual formats of patient-identifiable information may not be caught and removed. Text that still contains patient details may then be sent to external cloud services. One service is based in the UK (AWS, London). Another is based in Sweden (Azure), which is lawful under UK data transfer rules for the European Economic Area. If a valid data processing agreement is not in place with each provider, this transfer may breach UK data protection law.
update_risk.harm_description: A patient's confidential health information could be shared with an external company without proper legal agreements in place. This could breach the patient's right to confidentiality. It may also break UK data protection law (UK GDPR), which requires a completed Data Protection Impact Assessment before processing sensitive health data. The Information Commissioner's Office could investigate and issue a significant fine.

A separate test environment uses its own credentials and never handles real patient data, keeping live patient information away from testing activity (DI-2E40F292). The system flags data quality problems, including gaps in information removal, and records whether each check passed or failed so the team can review issues (DI-FC80B65A). Clinicians must actively confirm they have seen any warnings about data gaps before the system continues, creating a pause point if a problem is detected (DI-00E16F9E). Every clinical statement the system produces is linked back to the original source text in the patient record, so reviewers can check exactly what information was used (DI-740BE510). Reviewers can also select and highlight the exact section of the note the AI used, making it easier to spot if sensitive details were included (DI-E81545BE). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter. Additional controls are being identified.

For example, 'consider starting metformin' or 'call 999 if chest pain develops' describe things that have not happened yet. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible may label these as present findings. Those findings can then be saved into the patient record as if they were confirmed.

In the setting where a clinician reviews suggestions, the wrong suggestions still appear and waste the reviewer's time.

Safety-netting symptoms, such as chest pain to watch for, may be coded as findings the patient already has. This creates false diagnoses in the patient record. The system shows clinicians a plain-language summary of any coded finding before it is saved. This gives the reviewing clinician a clear chance to spot and reject incorrect suggestions at every review session (DI-66F1B177). A character-level locator ties each AI-extracted finding back to the exact words in the original note. This lets the reviewing clinician see the source sentence and judge whether the finding is real, every time a suggestion is made (DI-A0C90595). A configurable follow-up time window flags outstanding findings and places them on a worklist. The clinical team reviews this worklist at agreed intervals to catch any incorrectly coded items before they affect patient care (DI-4C73DC01). update_risk.title: An AI-suggested text alias causes the system to wrongly flag a clinical term in patient notes
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-003. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-003
update_risk.hazard_description: The system uses an AI tool to suggest extra text aliases for a clinical code. For example, it might suggest 'SOB' as an alias for 'Shortness of Breath'. But 'SOB' can mean something else entirely in UK clinical notes. If an administrator accepts an ambiguous or overly broad alias, the system will treat that phrase as a match for the clinical code whenever it appears in any patient's notes.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: An administrator opens the terminology settings screen and uses the AI button to suggest new text aliases for a clinical code. The AI tool returns a phrase that is ambiguous or too generic. The administrator accepts it without realising the risk. From that point on, the AI tool that reads notes treats every occurrence of that phrase as a match for the clinical code. In fully automated mode the system may save that code directly to the patient record. In review mode it sends the match to a clinician for checking.
update_risk.harm_description: If the system saves the wrong clinical code directly to a patient record, that patient's record becomes inaccurate. This could distort disease registers and population health figures used to plan care. Even in review mode, clinicians waste time checking false matches, and there is a risk that a busy reviewer accepts a wrong code without noticing the error.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, before any clinical code is saved to a patient record, a reviewer must individually approve it. No code is saved automatically without this step (DI-4247C7E5). This check is carried out by a trained reviewer for every proposed code, every time. Second, when the AI tool reads notes and finds a match, it records a confidence score and shows exactly where in the notes the match was found. This helps reviewers spot weak or unlikely matches (DI-31126C6C). Third, the system is tested regularly against a set of examples checked by an expert. It must reach a minimum accuracy level before it is used in practice. This test is run by the technical team before each release (DI-12015DBC). Fourth, the review screen shows the reviewer the context around each match, including whether the term was recorded as present, absent, or possible. This helps the reviewer judge whether the match makes clinical sense (DI-375C7EB1). Fifth, the review screen also shows which text alias triggered the match and flags any known issues with that alias. This lets the reviewer or administrator remove a problem alias quickly (DI-4221A226). Sixth, a coding correction review step lets a clinician challenge and correct any code that has been saved in error, with full checks against the terminology list (DI-1B8AC856). Seventh, the AI tool that suggests aliases is restricted to producing aliases only within the correct clinical category for each code. This reduces the chance of a wildly inappropriate alias being suggested (DI-C899D282). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

update_risk.title: AI tool matches clinical text to the wrong type of clinical code — error not flagged
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-003. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-003
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes gives each piece of clinical text a category label, such as 'finding', 'disorder', or 'procedure'. A separate part of the AI workflow then matches that text to a clinical code. Sometimes the clinical code it picks belongs to a different category than the label. For example, the word 'pain' is labelled as a 'disorder' but matched to a 'finding' code. The system accepts this mismatch without raising an alert.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinical note contains the word 'pain'. The AI tool labels it as a 'disorder'. The AI workflow finds a high-confidence 'finding' code for pain and accepts it without checking that the categories match. In fully automated mode, this wrongly categorised code is saved directly into the patient record. In review mode, the code appears correct on screen and the reviewing clinician may approve it without realising the category is wrong.
update_risk.harm_description: First, clinical codes in the patient record are assigned to the wrong category. This reduces the accuracy of the patient's coded record. Second, in fully automated mode, these wrong codes enter the patient record and may affect quality measures, disease statistics, and any alerts or decision support tools that rely on correct coding. Third, in review mode, a clinician may approve the wrong code because the error is not visible, meaning the patient's long-term record contains inaccurate information that could influence future care.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The AI workflow applies separate confidence thresholds for each clinical code category. It combines the category label confidence with the code-matching confidence before accepting a result. If either score is too low, the match is rejected automatically (DI-F0B8A7B0). A disorder-specific check runs as a final step. If this check fails, the system records a clear failed verdict and does not pass the code forward (DI-9D967259). The AI tool that reads notes records a full confidence score and source information for every code it proposes, so reviewers can see exactly how confident the system was and where the text came from (DI-31126C6C). Each coding proposal on the review screen shows the AI tool's context label and the supporting text, so the reviewing clinician can see why the code was suggested (DI-375C7EB1). All coding proposals must be individually approved by a reviewer before they are saved to the final record (DI-DI-4247C7E5). The system is tested against a set of examples checked by an expert before release. It must reach a minimum accuracy score of 0.85 on clinical coding before it can be used (DI-12015DBC). When a reviewer corrects a code, the system checks that the correction is valid and consistent with related codes before saving it (DI-1B8AC856). The AI tool uses a two-model approach where both models must agree before a code is accepted, reducing the chance of a single model making an unchecked error (DI-80DD8A47). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data on coding category mismatches every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

update_risk.title: AI audit tool enters a runaway loop and generates unexpected cloud computing costs
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI audit tool can get stuck in a repeating loop when checking patient records. Each loop adds more computing costs. Without a firm limit on how many loops are allowed, a single patient record could trigger hundreds of repeated checks.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: When the AI audit tool checks a large batch of patient records, it may run without any limit on how many times it repeats its checks. This can happen across hundreds or thousands of records at once. The total computing cost can far exceed the approved budget. This may cause unexpected charges and could slow down or stop other clinical services that share the same system.
update_risk.harm_description: Unexpected and potentially large financial charges from cloud computing use. Other clinical services that rely on the same system component may slow down or become unavailable. Improvements to the quality of examples used to teach the AI may be delayed if the process is stopped due to overspend.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The AI audit tool has a built-in limit on how many times it can repeat a check, and a cost cap that stops it spending beyond an approved budget. The team configures and monitors these limits (DI-54D00E21). The audit programme settings, including these limits, can be adjusted at any time without a full system redeployment, so the team can respond quickly if costs rise unexpectedly (DI-CD931485). A quality report checks that enough safety-critical records have been reviewed before the audit run is accepted; this acts as an early warning if a run has failed or been cut short (DI-AE477327). All audit activity is recorded in a log that the team can review to spot runaway loops or unusual cost patterns (DI-09E26C1D). Patient record data is handled through a standard, controlled system component, which limits the volume of data that can be sent into the AI tool in a single run (DI-1795254D). The clinical safety committee reviews cost reports and loop-limit breach logs every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

update_risk.title: AI tool suggests wrong clinical code, which could enter the teaching examples used to train the system
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-036. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-036
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI workflow uses two AI components working together to suggest clinical codes for patient record labels. The smaller AI component looks up codes and passes results to the larger one. The smaller component may misread the lookup results or invent code information that was not there. The larger component may then accept this wrong suggestion with high confidence.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: During a routine check of patient record labels, the smaller AI component returns a wrong clinical code pairing. The larger AI component accepts it confidently. If a reviewer approves this without checking carefully, or if a future software change removes the protection that stops automatic edits, the wrong clinical code could be saved into the examples used to teach the AI. This would teach the AI to code similar records incorrectly in future.
update_risk.harm_description: The AI tool that reads clinical notes could learn to apply wrong clinical codes to patient records. This could distort audit results and pathway coding for primary care patients. Clinicians and managers relying on those coded records could make decisions based on inaccurate information.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: An automated audit checks all teaching-example labels and flags problems for human review rather than fixing them automatically (DI-CFA65509). This runs continuously as part of the AI workflow. Any suggested change to a clinical code is always sent to a human reviewer and can never be applied automatically (DI-922114AE). The clinical safety team sets and monitors this rule. The AI workflow has strict limits on how many steps it can take and how much resource it can use, preventing runaway or unchecked activity (DI-54D00E21). These limits are configured by the technical team and reviewed regularly. All AI suggestions, including clinical code changes, go into a single review queue where reviewers can correct them, and those corrections are stored to improve future performance (DI-890BE989). Reviewers manage this queue as part of normal working. A separate check confirms that labels with multiple codes are recorded correctly (DI-EE80C271). This check runs automatically on each update. Before any update to the AI tool goes live, it must achieve at least 85 per cent accuracy on a set of labels checked by an expert clinician (DI-12015DBC). The clinical safety team runs this quality gate before each release. The system logs how often reviewers change or override AI suggestions, and the clinical safety officer has a dedicated view to spot signs that reviewers are accepting suggestions without adequate scrutiny (DI-22D862B0). The clinical safety committee reviews these metrics every quarter to confirm all controls are working as intended.

update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: gap. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: Each night, the system contacts NHS Digital to refresh the list of GP practices, PCNs, and other organisations. If that connection fails, the system may record the update as successful even though no new data was downloaded. Clinicians and managers then continue working with organisation information that could be weeks out of date, including organisations that have since closed or merged.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: During the scheduled nightly update, the NHS Digital organisation service is unavailable. The system receives errors for every request but records the update as complete and raises no alert. The next morning, clinicians use the system without knowing that organisation names, types, and closure statuses may no longer be correct.
update_risk.harm_description: Clinical audit records may be linked to the wrong organisation, or to one that no longer exists. This produces inaccurate pathway performance figures and sends clinical governance reports to the wrong team, delaying oversight of patient care quality.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
