update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The system records a full audit trail showing which organisation data was used for each audit result and when it was last updated. The clinical safety team can review this trail to spot gaps in data freshness (DI-09E26C1D). Pathway performance figures are built from the NHS Digital organisation hierarchy, so any mismatch between stored and current organisation data becomes visible when metrics are reviewed at practice, PCN, and ICB level (DI-B9109EF5). The system exports audit results through a standard clinical data interface, and the receiving system can flag records that carry stale organisation details (DI-1795254D). A continuous quality monitoring process tracks coding accuracy and raises an alert if figures fall outside expected ranges, which can indicate that organisation data is wrong (DI-1126FFD1). The deployment status panel shows the outcome of recent system updates, allowing reviewers to see whether the last nightly organisation update completed correctly (DI-6EA84931). The clinical safety committee reviews these controls and their effectiveness every quarter.

update_risk.title: Auto-correction picks the wrong clinical code for a term
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: When the AI tool that reads notes tries to fix a clinical term, it may choose a code that looks similar but means something different. This can happen silently, with no alert to the person reviewing the work.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The AI workflow automatically corrects a clinical term and links it to the wrong clinical code. The correct code is replaced without any warning. The expert-checked examples used to teach the AI then carry this wrong code. The team does not know the error has happened.
update_risk.harm_description: The AI learns from examples that contain the wrong clinical code. Over time, its accuracy falls. It may then pull incorrect information from patient notes, which could lead to a patient's condition being missed or wrongly recorded in their record.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system shows reviewers every clinical term alongside the codes that depend on it, so they can spot mismatches during the coding correction review. A trained clinician or coder carries out this check each time a correction is made (DI-4221A226). Second, each coding correction goes through a structured review that checks both the linked terms and the clinical code itself against the approved code list. A trained reviewer completes this check before any correction is saved (DI-1B8AC856). Third, the AI workflow must reach a minimum accuracy score on expert-checked examples before any updated coding is accepted. The clinical informatics team runs this quality gate before each model update (DI-12015DBC). Fourth, the interface for adding or changing clinical terms shows how often each term appears and blocks duplicate entries. Any person making changes uses this interface, and the system enforces these rules automatically at the point of entry (DI-30D95132). Fifth, an automated check reviews all expert-checked training examples, flags any that look wrong, limits how many can be auto-fixed at once, and places the rest in a queue for human review. The clinical informatics team monitors this queue on an ongoing basis (DI-CFA65509). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

update_risk.hazardous_situation: Examples used to teach the AI, and the expert-checked examples used to test it, are stored in the system's knowledge store. These records may still contain a patient number, a visit reference, or an organisation code. If a researcher or developer exports this data, they could link the clinical text back to an individual patient.

update_risk.title: AI-generated clinical rule criteria may be wrong or incomplete
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-065. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: partial. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-065
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads clinical guidelines can produce matching rules that contain wrong clinical codes, missing exclusion criteria, or conditions that are inverted so that present means absent and vice versa. If a rule like this is approved and activated, the system may wrongly match patients to a guideline recommendation, or fail to match patients who should be flagged.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The AI tool generates a clinical matching rule with a wrong clinical code or an inverted condition. An administrator reviews the rule but does not spot the error. The system activates the faulty rule. When a patient's record is checked against the rule, the system either flags the patient incorrectly or misses a flag that should have been raised. In a two-week-wait cancer pathway, a missed flag means a patient may not receive an urgent referral.
update_risk.harm_description: A patient on a two-week-wait cancer pathway either misses an urgent referral they need, or receives a referral that is not clinically appropriate. Missing an urgent cancer referral poses a direct risk to the patient's safety and could delay diagnosis of a serious condition.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the AI tool records exactly which part of the source guideline it used and which version of its instructions it followed when creating each rule candidate. This gives reviewers a clear audit trail to check the AI's working (DI-147C8EF0). Second, every AI-generated rule candidate must pass through a mandatory review queue before it can be activated. A clinician or administrator must make an explicit decision to approve or reject each candidate, and the system keeps a two-way link between the original source and the approved rule so the decision can always be traced (DI-F94EB13F). Third, the AI tool is prevented from generating direct diagnostic or treatment recommendations on its own; it only produces structured rule candidates for human review, which limits the impact of any single error (DI-A3107424). Fourth, when a referral rule is being reviewed, the system shows the reviewer the eligibility criteria and comparable patient outcomes side by side, making it easier to spot a rule that does not match clinical intent (DI-6C5D77CA). Fifth, the system can run two independent AI models and compare their outputs before a candidate rule is put forward for review; differences between the two models highlight potential errors for the reviewer (DI-80DD8A47). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs from the review queue and checks that all controls are working as intended every quarter.

update_risk.hazardous_situation: An administrator approves new clinical rules but does not complete the step needed to activate them. The system continues checking patients against the old rules only. The newly approved rules are silently ignored during patient pathway checks.
update_risk.harm_description: Patients are checked against out-of-date clinical rules. The system may miss patients who should be referred or flagged under the new guidance. This could delay appropriate referrals for those patients.

update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system uses a verified deployment package to confirm that only approved, checked rule sets are loaded into the live system. update_risk.title: A drop in coding accuracy goes unnoticed for several weeks, letting incorrect patient records build up.
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-079. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-079
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes and assigns clinical codes can develop a systematic error. This may happen after a software update, a change in how notes are written, or a new type of consultation. The weekly check that spots these errors may miss a problem that starts mid-week. If the weekly check fails to run at all, no alert is raised and no one is told.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: Coding quality falls across many patient records. The weekly accuracy check either fails to run due to a technical fault or runs but does not spot the problem. No alert reaches clinical staff or the operations team. Patients accumulate incorrect or missing clinical codes in their records for several weeks until a manual clinical review finds the problem.
update_risk.harm_description: Patients with incorrect or missing clinical codes may receive the wrong clinical decision or be placed in the wrong triage group. They may be missed by recall searches for long-term condition reviews. If serious conditions such as cancer, safeguarding concerns, or mental health problems are not coded correctly, referrals or follow-up may be delayed.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Six controls reduce this risk. First, the system continuously measures coding accuracy and raises an alert if it detects a drop; the AI workflow runs this check automatically and without interruption (DI-1126FFD1). Second, the system checks how often each type of clinical code is used and raises an alert if the pattern changes beyond a set threshold; the operations team can adjust that threshold; this check runs automatically each week (DI-37315D03). Third, when a drift alert is raised, the system records the reason and stores a full history of all alerts for two years in a way that cannot be altered; the operations team reviews this log (DI-B1E0EE52). Fourth, the system automatically checks that coded consultations follow clinical guidelines; this check runs on every coded encounter as it is processed (DI-2AFF691F). Fifth, a registry of guideline monitoring rules is kept under clinical change control; it holds the full context of every alert and sets out who must be told and when; the clinical safety team maintains this registry and reviews it when guidelines change (DI-ED3A89F5). Sixth, before any update goes live, the AI tool that assigns clinical codes must reach a minimum accuracy score on a set of encounters checked by an expert; if it does not reach that score, the update is blocked; the clinical safety team runs this check before every release (DI-12015DBC). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all six controls are working at least every quarter.

update_risk.title: Too many false alerts cause staff to ignore them, so a real coding failure goes unnoticed.
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-016 FMEA-045. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-016 FMEA-045
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that checks coding quality can fire alerts too often. This happens when its trigger threshold is set too low, or when normal week-to-week variation sets it off. Staff who see repeated false alerts learn to dismiss them without looking. When a real problem occurs, such as cancer codes being missed, the alert is dismissed in the same way. The problem then continues for up to 14 days before the system automatically pauses the AI workflow.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The AI quality checker sends repeated alerts that turn out to be false alarms. Operations staff stop reading them properly and click to acknowledge without investigating. A genuine coding failure, for example cancer or safeguarding codes being missed, triggers an alert that staff dismiss within minutes. The coding failure continues for up to 14 days until the system automatically pauses. If staff manually override that pause, the failure continues even longer.
update_risk.harm_description: Serious coding gaps, covering cancer, safeguarding, and mental health, go unnoticed for weeks. Patients whose records are affected do not get the timely clinical follow-up that the correct code would have triggered.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The AI workflow uses configurable thresholds to suppress alerts that fall within normal variation, reducing the number of false alarms that reach staff (DI-79509E39). The clinical safety team reviews and adjusts these thresholds regularly. The system continuously monitors coding quality and sends a regression alert whenever accuracy drops below an agreed level (DI-1126FFD1). The clinical safety team reviews these metrics at least monthly. If an alert is not acknowledged within the agreed time, the system automatically pauses the AI workflow and escalates to a senior responsible person (DI-5A802C83). This escalation runs without any manual step. Every alert acknowledgement is recorded with the clinician or operator identity and a timestamp, creating a permanent log that cannot be altered (DI-B46AD5CE). The clinical safety team audits this log quarterly. When a regression alert fires, staff must label the root cause before closing it. All alert history is kept for two years and cannot be deleted (DI-B1E0EE52). The clinical safety team uses this history to spot patterns of alert fatigue. Safety-critical entity types, including cancer and safeguarding codes, are counted and checked against a minimum quality gate before any update to the AI workflow goes live (DI-AE477327). The clinical safety team runs this check before every release. Any change to the coding rules used by the AI tool must pass through a staged review, be approved, and be version-controlled so it can be rolled back if a regression is detected (DI-9FD54AD6). The clinical safety committee reviews all of these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: A false diagnosis code stays in a patient record and leads to wrong clinical decisions or unnecessary follow-up.
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-045. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-045
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes can wrongly add a diagnosis the patient does not have. This is called overcoding. If the audit spots the error but no one reviews it quickly, the false code stays in the record. Clinical staff may then act on it, affecting treatment decisions, waiting-list membership, or care pathways.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The audit finds an overcoded diagnosis — for example, a cancer code on a record where the patient does not have cancer. The system creates an urgent review task. That task gets lost in a general queue, or the reviewer is on leave. After 48 hours, no safety alert is raised because the alert rules do not check whether urgent overcoding tasks have been completed on time. The false code stays in the record for days or weeks. Clinicians reading the record see the false code and make decisions based on it.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient may receive unnecessary tests, referrals, or treatment based on a condition they do not have. They may also suffer significant worry or distress from a false serious-illness code. The false code may also place the patient on the wrong care register or direct them down the wrong care pathway.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system holds all urgent overcoding review tasks in a dedicated queue with a strict time limit and automatic escalation if the task is not completed on time. The clinical informatics team monitors this queue daily (DI-5E1BA369). Second, a human-review gate stops any audit findings from being used or reported until a trained reviewer has checked and approved them. The clinical coding team runs this check before each audit report is released (DI-BD696225). Third, a separate accuracy check compares the results from the AI tool that reads notes against a second set of rules to catch disagreements before any code reaches the patient record. The clinical safety team reviews these comparison results weekly (DI-F298AE65). Fourth, a change-control gate requires review and approval before any update to the way the AI tool labels diagnoses can go live, with the ability to roll back if a problem is found. The clinical safety officer approves each change (DI-9FD54AD6). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all four controls are working as intended every quarter.

update_risk.hazard_description: When a reviewer links a phrase to a clinical code, the AI tool saves that link and uses it automatically for every future patient record containing the same phrase. If the reviewer picks the wrong code, no second check happens. Every record with that phrase is then coded incorrectly until someone notices.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A reviewer links the phrase 'chest tightness' to the clinical code for anxiety instead of angina. The AI tool immediately saves this link. All future patient records containing 'chest tightness' are automatically coded as anxiety. Patients with possible heart symptoms are miscoded for weeks until a routine audit spots the pattern.
update_risk.harm_description: Many patient records carry the wrong clinical code for the same phrase. Patients with that phrase may be sent down the wrong care pathway, receive the wrong clinical decisions, or be missed when the system searches for patients with a specific condition such as angina.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)

update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system holds any new phrase-to-code link in a staging area before it goes live. A second reviewer must approve the change, and the system keeps a full version history so any wrong link can be rolled back quickly (DI-9FD54AD6). The clinical safety team checks this gate is working every quarter. Second, when a reviewer is deciding on a code, the screen shows how many patient records use that phrase. This helps the reviewer understand the impact of their choice before approving it. The system also blocks duplicate links from being created (DI-30D95132). Third, every coded entry in a patient record keeps a clear link back to the original note and the source of the code. This makes it straightforward to trace and correct a wrong code if one is found (DI-740BE510). Fourth, the AI tool cannot publish any coded interpretation without a reviewer making an active decision. No code reaches a patient record without human sign-off (DI-604767B1). Fifth, the review screen shows whether a change has already been deployed to live records. Reviewers can see the potential reach of a decision before they approve it (DI-6EA84931). Sixth, the review screen shows which patient records and phrases depend on the link being changed. Reviewers can see the full impact before approving (DI-4221A226). Seventh, after codes are saved to patient records, an automated check runs to flag any coded entries that do not match accepted clinical guidelines. This catches patterns of miscoding early (DI-2AFF691F). The clinical safety committee reviews audit results from all these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: Fixing a wrong clinical code link stops future errors but leaves past patient records with the wrong code.
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: gap. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: Sometimes a link between a written term and a clinical code is found to be wrong. The AI tool that reads notes can be told to stop using that link. This prevents new errors. However, every patient record already coded using that wrong link keeps the incorrect code. There is no automatic way to find those records or correct them.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A wrong code link goes unnoticed for three weeks. During that time, 47 patient encounters are saved with the wrong clinical code. A reviewer spots the error and removes the link. Future encounters are now coded correctly. But those 47 records still show the wrong code. No alert or review task is created for them. Any clinician looking at those 47 records will see the wrong code and may act on it.
update_risk.harm_description: Past patient records carry wrong clinical codes. Depending on the clinical area, this could affect how urgent a referral appears, whether a patient is added to a disease register, which care pathway they follow, or the accuracy of audit data. The more records affected and the more serious the clinical area, the greater the potential harm to patients.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Five controls reduce the chance of harm from past records carrying a wrong clinical code. First, the system shows clinicians a referral triage view with eligibility rules and comparable outcomes, helping them spot when a referral decision looks unusual; this runs automatically each time a referral is reviewed (DI-6C5D77CA). Second, the system automatically checks whether coded encounters follow current clinical guidelines; this check runs on every coded encounter and flags those that do not match expected patterns (DI-2AFF691F). Third, the coding correction review page shows how often a clinical code has been used over time; a reviewer can see a sudden spike in use that may signal a wrong code link has been active, and this display is available to any clinician or coder opening the review page (DI-22F4E3CE). Fourth, the coding correction review page also shows which written terms depend on a given code link; this helps reviewers understand how many records may be affected before and after a correction, and is available on demand to reviewers (DI-4221A226). Fifth, any change to a code link must pass through a staged review and approval process before it takes effect; changes are versioned and can be rolled back if needed, and this gate is applied every time a code link is created or changed (DI-9FD54AD6). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and flagged encounters every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: Patient details leak into AI teaching files, causing a data breach.
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The system is designed to remove patient details from clinical notes before storing or exporting them. If this removal step fails, real patient details — such as a name, NHS number, date of birth, or address — can end up saved inside the system or written into files used to teach the AI. Those files are then accessible to people who have no right to see patient records.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient's name, NHS number, date of birth, or address appears in a clinical note. The tool that removes patient details misses it — for example, because it does not recognise that type of detail, or because the sentence is written in an unusual way. The raw detail is saved into the system. When teaching files are later created, a second check also misses it. The patient's detail ends up inside a teaching file that AI developers can read.
update_risk.harm_description: A patient's private details are shared with AI developers without a lawful reason under UK data protection law. This is a reportable data breach under the Data Protection Act 2018. The patient's privacy is violated. The organisation may face investigation and enforcement action by the Information Commissioner's Office. Commissioners and patients may lose trust in the service.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: IG/Security (GDPR + DCB0129).
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, before any teaching file is created, an automatic check scans the file for patient details and stops the export if any are found, logging the problem for review by the clinical safety team (DI-452D4303). This check runs every time a teaching file is produced. Second, the system stores a protected set of teaching examples that are kept separate and cannot be changed, so there is always a clean reference set to compare against (DI-BB64E479). This separation is set up once and maintained permanently by the technical team. Third, the system records accuracy figures for each type of detail the removal tool is supposed to catch, and stores these results each time the AI is retrained (DI-CE0A08E5). The clinical safety team reviews these figures after every retraining run to spot any drop in performance. Fourth, if an export fails or a problem is logged, the system provides a list of affected records with the reason for failure, and allows the team to reprocess them with one action (DI-69CE20C1). The clinical safety team reviews this list at least weekly. Fifth, the system exports teaching examples in a format that preserves all detail labels without loss, so that any remaining patient details are not hidden during review (DI-6EFD68D0). The technical team checks this format is working correctly with each new software release. The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: Test patient records used during AI training, making accuracy results misleading and hiding true performance.
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: FMEA-037. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk | Added FMEA link: FMEA-037 (holdout leakage)
update_risk.hazard_description: Some patient records are set aside as test records, so the AI tool that reads notes is never trained on them. This keeps the test fair. If those test records are accidentally included in training, the AI has already seen its own test. Its accuracy scores look good, but they no longer reflect how it will perform on real, unseen records.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A change to the system removes the filter that keeps test records separate. Test records are included when training data is collected. The AI tool that reads notes trains on these records. When the team checks accuracy using the same records, the scores are high because the AI has already seen them. The team concludes the AI is ready for use. In practice, the AI performs worse than the scores suggested. This includes detecting safety-critical conditions such as cancer, safeguarding concerns, and mental health problems.
update_risk.harm_description: The AI tool is released believing it meets the required accuracy standard. Its true real-world accuracy is unknown and may be below that standard. It may miss clinical codes for cancer, safeguarding, or mental health in patient records. No warning is given to the clinician. A patient's condition may go unrecorded and unacted upon.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls are in place to reduce this risk. First, the training data is kept in a fixed, separate store with an immutable barrier between training records and test records. No training run can access test records. The AI development team maintains this separation at all times (DI-BB64E479). Second, before any training run is approved, an automated check counts how many safety-critical records, covering cancer, safeguarding, and mental health, are present in the training set. If the count does not meet the required threshold, training is blocked. The AI development team runs this check before every training cycle (DI-AE477327). Third, after the AI tool is deployed, an automated check runs against coded patient records to confirm the AI is still performing as expected. The AI development team runs this check on a scheduled basis (DI-2AFF691F). Fourth, the system monitors how often each type of clinical code appears over time. If the frequency drifts beyond a set limit, an alert is raised. The AI development team reviews these alerts on a scheduled basis (DI-37315D03). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all four controls are working every quarter.

update_risk.title: Admin appointment details are saved as clinical findings in the patient record
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk | Workshop flag: Dedup Auditor flagged R-054 and R-033 as possible merge (non-clinical text miscoded as finding). Medium confidence - retain both.
update_risk.hazard_description: Patient records in EMIS include administrative lines such as timestamps, staff names, and appointment confirmations. The AI tool that reads notes may treat these lines as clinical content. If it does, it can attach clinical codes to them — for example, codes meaning 'seen in GP surgery' — even though no clinician wrote a clinical finding. These codes come from admin data, not from a doctor's assessment.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: When the AI workflow processes an encounter, it may pick up an admin header line and treat it as a clinical statement. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible then assigns a clinical code to that line. The code is saved into the patient's clinical record as if it were a real finding. This can inflate the count of coded findings in the record. Audit dashboards may then show misleading results. A clinician reviewing the record may accept the code without realising it came from an admin line rather than a clinical note.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient's clinical record contains clinical codes that are not supported by any clinical note. Audit quality reports become inaccurate. When a clinician reviews and approves a code that came from an admin line, that approval may also be used as an example to teach the AI — making the problem worse over time. If the system is running without clinician review, the patient record is changed directly on the basis of admin text, not clinical judgement.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the AI workflow stores the exact words it used as evidence alongside every clinical code it assigns. This lets a reviewing clinician see at a glance whether the evidence is a clinical note or an admin line. The clinical safety team checks this is working every quarter (DI-23822663). Second, every clinical code is shown to the reviewer with a plain-English explanation of what the code means and where the evidence came from. This helps clinicians spot codes that do not match any real clinical finding. The clinical safety team audits a sample of reviewed codes monthly (DI-66F1B177). Third, the review screen shows the reviewer the exact evidence phrase and the AI's judgement — whether the finding was present, absent, or possible — for every code on the review card. This makes it easier to reject codes sourced from admin lines. The clinical safety team checks the review screen design every quarter (DI-375C7EB1). Fourth, the AI workflow runs two independent checks on every code: the AI tool that reads notes and a separate rules-based check. If the two checks disagree, the code is flagged for human review rather than saved automatically. The clinical safety team reviews disagreement rates monthly (DI-F298AE65). Fifth, the system tracks coding accuracy continuously and raises an alert if the rate of unexpected or low-quality codes rises above a set threshold. The clinical safety team reviews these alerts weekly (DI-1126FFD1). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls together every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: A common GP abbreviation is matched to the wrong clinical code
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk | Workshop flag: Dedup Auditor - keep both but cross-link. R-055 is a high-severity subset of R-004.
update_risk.hazard_description: GPs often use short abbreviations that can mean more than one thing. For example, CA can mean cancer or calcium. NAD can mean no abnormality detected or a body chemical. MSK can mean a musculoskeletal problem or a specialty. The AI tool that reads notes may pick the wrong meaning if the surrounding text does not make the intended meaning clear. The wrong clinical code is then saved to the patient record.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: The AI tool that reads notes pulls a short abbreviation from a consultation entry. It passes the abbreviation to the part of the AI workflow that matches words to clinical codes. That part does not have enough surrounding detail, such as the body site or organ, to choose the correct code. It returns a biochemistry code, a vague general code, or a specialty label instead of the clinically correct one. The wrong code is saved into the patient record and shown on the clinical review screen. This could affect how the patient is coded, influence GP contract reporting, and shape future clinical decisions.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient record holds the wrong clinical code. If a cancer or serious disease code is added in error, the patient may be referred or investigated unnecessarily. If a genuine cancer or long-term condition code is missed entirely, the patient may not receive the follow-up, monitoring, or treatment they need. Adding a code in error carries the greater immediate risk because it can trigger urgent clinical actions based on incorrect information.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the AI workflow checks that any clinical code it suggests is supported by the specific words found in the notes. This stops codes being suggested when the surrounding text is too vague to confirm the meaning. The clinical informatics team sets this up as part of the system build, and it runs automatically every time the AI processes a note (DI-C899D282). Second, the AI tool that reads notes and a separate checking step must both agree on whether a condition is present, absent, or possible before a code is suggested. If they disagree, the code is held back for a clinician to review. The clinical informatics team configures this check, and it runs automatically on every entry (DI-F298AE65). Third, the clinical review screen shows the clinician the exact words from the notes that led to each suggested code, together with a label saying whether the condition was recorded as present, absent, or possible. The clinician can see this information before accepting or rejecting any code. The development team builds this into the review screen, and it is visible at every coding review (DI-375C7EB1). Fourth, the review screen also shows which other words or phrases in the notes the suggested code depends on, so the clinician can judge whether the full context supports the code. The development team builds this into the review screen, and it is visible at every coding review (DI-4221A226). Fifth, a coding correction workflow lets clinicians flag and correct any wrong code. When a correction is made, the system checks that related codes in the record are still consistent. The clinical informatics team maintains this workflow, and it is available to clinicians at all times (DI-1B8AC856). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data on coding corrections and disagreements between the AI steps every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

update_risk.title: The AI workflow applies a wrong clinical code change to a patient record
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-050 | Split out: FMEA-050 moved to new R-LEO-AI-160 per Dedup Auditor
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI workflow misreads an audit finding. The AI tool that checks the proposed change then agrees with the wrong answer. This causes a clinical code link in the patient record to be wrongly deleted, added, or altered.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient's record ends up with a wrong clinical code. A real active diagnosis may be removed. A false diagnosis may be added. Or a current condition may be wrongly marked as past history. A clinician then reads the record and makes a clinical decision based on that wrong information.
update_risk.harm_description: A wrong clinical code can lead to a patient receiving the wrong treatment. They may miss preventive care or be sent down the wrong care pathway. In high-risk areas such as cancer, mental health, or safeguarding, this could delay a diagnosis or delay the start of treatment.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The system shows the reviewing clinician the original code, the proposed replacement code, the clinical concept, and the reason for the change in a structured display, so the clinician can spot errors before approving any change (DI-04105500). The review screen also shows how often each code has been used historically, helping the clinician judge whether a proposed change looks unusual (DI-22F4E3CE). Before any replacement code is accepted, the system checks that the code is current and valid in the clinical terminology, blocking out-of-date codes automatically (DI-26CBDB16). The review screen shows which words in the clinical notes the AI tool that reads notes used to identify the code, so the clinician can see whether the AI read the notes correctly (DI-4221A226). A dedicated review step brings together the code dependency information and the terminology validity check in one place, so the clinician has everything needed to make a safe decision (DI-1B8AC856). When a large number of coding changes are proposed at once, the system requires a second clinician to review and approve the batch before any changes are saved to patient records (DI-13F340B9). The AI tool that reads notes is designed to preserve clinical detail such as severity and certainty, reducing the risk that a specific diagnosis is replaced with a vague or wrong one (DI-6A0B55A4). The review screen shows the AI tool's decision about whether a condition is present, absent, or possible, alongside the supporting text from the notes, so the clinician can check the AI's reasoning (DI-375C7EB1). All patient record data coming into the system and all audit results leaving it pass through a validated system component, reducing the risk of data being corrupted in transit (DI-1795254D). A separate system component records a full history of every change, showing who proposed it and why, without exposing the full clinical record unnecessarily, so errors can be traced and investigated (DI-09E26C1D). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and any reported incidents every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: AI coding tool assigns a wrong clinical code without a clinician checking it first
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-058. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-058
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes picks the wrong clinical code, gets the context wrong (for example, marking a finding as absent when it is present), or misses a safety-critical finding entirely. The check that should block incorrect codes from being saved into the patient record fails to catch the error.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A consultation note contains a red-flag cancer symptom or a safeguarding concern. The AI tool that reads notes finds a plausible but wrong clinical code — for example, it codes a benign lesion instead of a suspected malignancy. The AI workflow rates its own confidence as high and passes the code through without triggering a human review. The wrong code is saved into the patient record. A clinical dashboard then shows the patient as lower risk than they truly are. The clinician does not escalate or refer the patient.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient's cancer referral is delayed or a safeguarding alert is missed. This can cause serious harm through late diagnosis or failure to protect a vulnerable person.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Seven controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool rates its own confidence and flags the context for every finding it identifies — for example, whether a condition is present, absent, or possible — so reviewers can see the basis for each code (DI-48AD06E5). Second, a separate check compares the context label produced by the AI tool that reads notes against the context label produced by the AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible; any mismatch is flagged before the code is saved (DI-F298AE65). Third, the coding review card shown to the clinician displays the context label and the exact text from the note that the AI used as evidence, so the clinician can judge whether the code is correct (DI-375C7EB1). Fourth, a human-review gate blocks any action — including saving codes — on unreviewed safety alerts; no code linked to a guideline alert reaches the patient record until a clinician approves it (DI-7913344A). Fifth, the system component that supplies clinical codes is kept up to date, and any change in a clinical code version triggers a blocking review before the update is applied (DI-553F50A2 and DI-B193C816). Sixth, the examples used to teach the AI are checked to ensure enough safety-critical findings are included; a quality gate stops training if the count falls below a safe threshold (DI-AE477327). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of flagged mismatches, human-review gate activations, and coding accuracy every quarter to confirm all controls are working.

update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-058. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-058
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes can find mentions of conditions that are recorded as absent, ruled out, or historical. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible must filter these out before creating a care pathway record. If this filtering fails, the system creates an active pathway record based on a condition the patient does not currently have.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician writes "no evidence of cancer" or "history of breast cancer (resolved)". The AI tool that reads notes correctly finds the cancer mention but the AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible does not filter it out. The system then creates an active cancer pathway record for that patient. A dashboard shows the patient as being on an active cancer pathway. A clinician may then arrange unnecessary follow-up or investigations for a condition the patient does not have.
update_risk.harm_description: A clinician may act on an incorrect active pathway record and arrange unnecessary tests or treatment for a patient who does not have the condition. Equally, if the filtering is set too broadly, real active pathways may be hidden, and a patient who needs follow-up may be missed. Both errors could cause the patient direct harm.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The system stores the exact words from the notes alongside every decision the AI tool makes about whether a condition is present, absent, or possible. This lets a clinician or reviewer check why a pathway record was created (DI-23822663). The coding review card shows the clinician the AI tool's decision and the supporting words from the notes, so errors can be spotted quickly during routine review (DI-375C7EB1). The AI workflow uses multi-type classification to handle overlapping clinical codes correctly, reducing the chance of a wrong pathway record being created in the first place (DI-DC61F5B6). Any pathway record that is flagged as potentially incorrect is blocked from appearing in reports until a clinician has reviewed and resolved the flag, preventing incorrect information from reaching clinical dashboards (DI-A0579B64). The system uses an up-to-date clinical coding reference so that code meanings are current and correctly interpreted (DI-553F50A2). A workflow is in place to manage changes to clinical coding releases and resolve any conflicts before they affect pathway records (DI-B193C816). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and flagged pathway records every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: Active cancer investigation wrongly closed because an unrelated test result is misread by the AI tool
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk | MERGED_IN: R-LEO-AI-061 (Cancer pathway incorrectly closed as completed after specialist letter when trea) per Dedup Auditor
update_risk.hazard_description: A clinical code meaning 'no evidence of cancer found' is used in many different situations. It can appear after a cervical smear, a routine health check, or a cancer pathway discharge. The AI tool that reads notes may search for this code across the whole patient record without checking the date. If it finds the code from an unrelated test, it can wrongly decide that an open cancer investigation has been resolved.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient has an open urgent two-week-wait breast cancer investigation started in July 2024. In 2026, a cervical smear result is recorded using the same clinical code for 'no cancer found'. Because the AI tool does not check whether the code relates to the breast investigation, it closes the breast investigation and marks it as resolved. The breast investigation disappears from the open cases dashboard. Clinicians reviewing open cancer cases can no longer see it.
update_risk.harm_description: The active breast cancer investigation is wrongly marked as finished. It is removed from the clinician review list. The patient may not receive timely follow-up. This increases the risk of a delayed cancer diagnosis, which could cause serious harm.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool that decides if a finding is present, absent, or possible displays its reasoning and the supporting evidence on a coding review card, so a clinician can see why the investigation was closed (DI-375C7EB1). This check runs each time the AI tool processes a patient record. Second, the system shows a plain-English summary of what each coded finding means, so reviewers can quickly spot if a code has been applied in the wrong context (DI-66F1B177). This is shown to the reviewing clinician every time a coded finding is displayed. Third, any episode the AI tool has flagged as uncertain is blocked from being reported as closed until a clinician resolves the flag (DI-A0579B64). This quality gate runs automatically before any episode status is finalised. Fourth, when clinical guidelines that underpin the AI rules are updated or withdrawn, the system enforces a review of all episodes that relied on those rules, preventing outdated rules from silently closing investigations (DI-F1A768AE). This runs whenever a guideline change is recorded. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and flag resolution rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

add_fmea_item.failure_mode: Historic specialist visits attributed to later same-site referrals, causing false stale episode status
add_fmea_item.failure_effect: A patient completes a breast cancer 2WW pathway in 2024 (specialist seen, no cancer found). A new breast referral is raised in 2025. During episode rebuild, the 2024 specialist visit is attributed to the 2025 episode. The 2025 episode is flagged stale_post_specialist (>90 days since "specialist visit"). The actual open pathway -- where the patient still needs a specialist appointment -- is auto-closed with a HITL flag instead of remaining in_progress for active follow-up.
add_fmea_item.failure_cause: The episode detection algorithm assigns specialist visit anchors to episode nodes using only a cancer-site keyword match, with no constraint that the visit date must fall after the episode referral date. A specialist visit from an earlier pathway is re-attributed to a later same-site episode.

update_risk.title: An old specialist visit is wrongly linked to a new referral, making an active pathway look finished
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes links specialist visits to a cancer pathway using only the cancer site (for example, breast). It does not check whether the visit happened before or after the referral was raised. This means a specialist visit from a completed old pathway can be wrongly attached to a new, still-open pathway for the same cancer site.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient finishes a breast cancer urgent referral pathway in 2024. A new breast referral is raised in 2025. When the AI workflow rebuilds the episode, it attaches the 2024 specialist visit to the 2025 pathway. The 2025 pathway then appears to have had a specialist visit over 90 days ago. The system marks it as stale and auto-closes it, adding it to the human review queue instead of keeping it open for active follow-up. The patient still needs a specialist appointment, but the pathway no longer shows as active.
update_risk.harm_description: An active cancer investigation pathway is wrongly closed. The patient may not receive a timely specialist review. Audit reports undercount open pathways and overcount completed ones. Clinicians reviewing the human review queue may not spot that this patient is still waiting and at risk.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the AI workflow only uses milestone dates that a human reviewer has accepted before calculating pathway timings. This stops wrongly dated visits from triggering a stale status. The clinical informatics team configures this gate, and it runs on every pathway rebuild (DI-EE4E6477). Second, a risk-scored change queue holds any auto-closure that would affect an active pathway. No change reaches live records until a reviewer approves it. The deployment team manages this queue continuously (DI-7C5EC850). Third, the system checks coding quality metrics automatically and raises an alert if accuracy drops or a pattern of wrong episode links appears. The clinical safety team reviews these alerts at least weekly (DI-1126FFD1). Fourth, an automated audit checks the examples used to teach the AI for labelling errors. It flags suspect labels for human review and limits how many it can correct on its own. The clinical informatics team runs this audit before each model update (DI-CFA65509). Fifth, before any pathway status changes, the system checks for conflicts with clinical guidelines and preserves an under-review status so the pathway stays available to clinicians while the conflict is resolved. The clinical safety team oversees this check on every release (DI-48ACD153). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all five controls are working every quarter.

update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-063. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-063
update_risk.hazard_description: After a patient sees a specialist, the AI tool reads the clinical notes to decide whether the outcome was cancer or benign. It may wrongly decide the outcome was benign. This can happen if notes about cancer treatment did not appear within six months, or if the outcome letter was private or hidden from the system.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient who has or may have cancer has their specialist episode wrongly labelled as benign. This label feeds into reporting dashboards. The episode may then be removed from the list of cases waiting for a human review. The quality lead sees the pathway as closed when it is not.
update_risk.harm_description: A cancer case that needs follow-up is missed. If no one reviews the pathway manually, the patient may not receive timely care. This could lead to serious harm from delayed cancer treatment.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)

The AI tool applies a clear status label to every episode, marking it as confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive rather than defaulting to benign when information is missing (DI-37DDAADE). The system shows the reviewing clinician guideline-recommended treatments alongside comparable patient outcomes, so gaps in the pathway are visible at a glance (DI-82D5359B). The system also flags recovery markers and compares the patient trajectory against similar cases, making it easier to spot when an expected cancer treatment pathway is absent (DI-49403C92). A structured multidisciplinary team summary template prompts the reviewer to work through a pathway checklist and compare the case against similar patients before closing it (DI-DBC2399F). update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-063. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-063
update_risk.hazard_description: A platform administrator uses a data-correction tool to delete consultations, change clinical findings, or update patient records. If used with wrong settings, this can corrupt the patient's clinical data.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: An administrator runs a data-correction action without checking the preview first, or enters the wrong settings. This can delete valid clinical information or write wrong clinical codes into the patient record. Downstream, this affects whether the system correctly identifies a cancer pathway, triggers safety-net alerts, or produces correct clinical codes for clinical users.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient's record holds wrong or missing information. This can mean the system shows the wrong cancer pathway status, misses a safety-net alert, or sends wrong clinical codes to clinicians. A patient could be harmed if their cancer care is delayed or a warning about their condition is not raised.

update_risk.title: Wrong cancer stage recorded at diagnosis
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes may assign the wrong stage group to a cancer diagnosis. This can happen when the notes use unusual wording, when the evidence is unclear, or when the rules for a specific cancer site are not matched correctly. For example, a late-stage cancer could be recorded as early-stage, or the other way round.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient's cancer episode is given the wrong stage group. Quality dashboards then show incorrect figures for early versus late diagnosis rates. Quality teams use these figures to judge how well the cancer pathway is performing, so they draw the wrong conclusions.
update_risk.harm_description: Quality teams make improvement decisions based on wrong data. Problems with late diagnosis are not spotted or acted on quickly enough. This delays action that could improve outcomes for future patients on the cancer pathway.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, a data quality dashboard tracks how often the staging rules produce a valid result, broken down by cancer programme and rule type. The clinical safety team reviews this regularly to spot unusual patterns or drops in accuracy (DI-E6A32FF5). Second, the AI tool stores the exact text from the notes that it used to decide the stage. Clinicians reviewing a record can see this evidence and check whether the decision was correct (DI-23822663). Third, cancer programme leads can update the staging rule sets without needing a software release. This means errors in the rules can be corrected quickly when they are found (DI-AA8014F9). Fourth, population-level pathway dashboards show local staging rates alongside national benchmarks. Unexpected differences alert quality teams to possible data errors (DI-BA2C8F3E). Fifth, programme leads can set thresholds that control when staging results are shown or suppressed, reducing the risk that unreliable results reach dashboards (DI-0D7DCC52). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-008 FMEA-037 | Data fix: FMEA-037 re-routed to R-LEO-AI-053 per Dedup Auditor | Split out: FMEA-008 moved to new R-LEO-AI-159 per Dedup Auditor
update_risk.hazard_description: The system shows auditors cancer episode information pulled from clinical notes by the AI tool that reads notes. This information includes cancer type, stage, key dates, and clinical codes. If the AI tool has made an error — for example, recording a benign finding as a cancer diagnosis — and the auditor does not spot the mistake before approving the episode, that wrong information enters the record as validated.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: An auditor opens a patient episode where the AI tool that reads notes has wrongly coded a benign finding as a cancer diagnosis, or missed a cancer diagnosis entirely. The auditor checks the coded summary but does not look at the original clinical notes to confirm it. The auditor marks the episode as reviewed and approved. That episode is then used to calculate how common certain cancers are across the practice population. Those figures are used to decide which GP referral pathways to prioritise.
update_risk.harm_description: Clinicians make referral and resource decisions based on cancer prevalence figures that contain undetected errors. Pathways may be under-prioritised or over-prioritised as a result. Patients in under-prioritised pathways may experience delayed diagnosis or delayed access to treatment.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The system blocks any approved episode from influencing pathway decisions until a human auditor has reviewed it. This human-review gate is built into the system and runs automatically for every episode (DI-7913344A). The AI tool that reads notes stores the exact text it used to reach each clinical decision, so auditors can check the original wording alongside the coded result. This is available on every episode at the point of review (DI-23822663). The system runs automatic quality checks on each episode, flagging unusual durations, missing key dates, and events recorded in the wrong order. These checks run automatically each time an episode is processed (DI-1206D9E8). A live performance dashboard shows auditors and the safety team how accurately the AI tool is performing across all episode types. It refreshes automatically and is available to the clinical team at all times (DI-067E471A). Any episode the system cannot process correctly appears in a failed episode list with a clear reason for failure. A member of the team can send it for reprocessing with one click, so no episode is silently lost (DI-69CE20C1). The accuracy of the AI tool is measured separately for each type of clinical information it extracts. These figures are recorded each time the AI is updated and are available for review at any time (DI-CE0A08E5). When the AI tool is retrained, only annotations checked by an expert are used, and any that do not align correctly with the original text are automatically excluded (DI-E7AFFDA5). The AI tool is retrained regularly using a structured improvement cycle that includes expert-checked examples and performance tracking over time (DI-37B3DC71). The clinical safety committee reviews audit completion rates, AI accuracy figures, and any flagged episodes every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

update_risk.title: Spinal level labels mistaken for cancer staging codes
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-039. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-039
update_risk.hazard_description: Spinal anatomy uses letter-number labels such as C3, T4, and L5 to describe vertebrae. Cancer staging also uses labels like T4 and N2 to describe tumour spread. The AI tool that reads notes cannot always tell these apart. When it sees 'T4' in a physiotherapy or back-pain note, it may treat it as a cancer staging code and save it to the patient record.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A GP writes a note about a patient's back or neck, for example 'C3-T4 facet areas' or 'NAGs C3'. The AI tool that reads notes picks out 'T4' as a separate item. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible does not have a rule to check whether 'T4' is a spinal level or a cancer stage. It assigns a cancer staging clinical code and saves it to the patient record. The cancer audit system then picks up this code as if the patient has a confirmed cancer stage.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient record now shows a cancer staging code that does not belong there. Cancer audit dashboards show the wrong stage distribution across the cancer pathway. Clinical quality teams may make incorrect improvement decisions based on this inaccurate data. Individual patients could also be incorrectly flagged as having a cancer stage, causing unnecessary concern or follow-up.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The AI workflow uses rules that constrain which clinical codes can be assigned based on the surrounding clinical context, reducing the chance that a spinal label is mapped to a cancer staging code (DI-3EA60D5A). This rule set is maintained by the clinical informatics team and reviewed whenever the AI workflow is updated. A separate gate checks and approves any change to the way staging surface forms are matched to clinical codes; changes must be reviewed, approved, and versioned before going live, and can be rolled back if a problem is found (DI-9FD54AD6). This gate is operated by the clinical safety team and runs for every proposed change. The AI tool that reads notes preserves the clinical context around each term, such as whether it appears in a musculoskeletal or oncology section, so that the correct clinical code can be chosen (DI-6A0B55A4). This is applied automatically during every note-reading process. The cohort builder applies rule-based checks across clinical codes, pathway stage, and patient details to catch records that do not fit expected patterns (DI-FE3FFE50). The clinical informatics team reviews cohort outputs at each audit cycle. The examples used to teach the AI are checked to ensure safety-critical entities such as cancer staging codes are represented accurately and in sufficient numbers, with a quality gate that blocks training if counts fall below a safe threshold (DI-AE477327). This check is run by the data science team before every training run. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs, cohort outputs, and gate reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: AI quality check removes correct clinical findings or adds ones not supported by the notes
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-007 FMEA-020. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-007 FMEA-020 | Workshop flag: Dedup Auditor flagged R-068 and R-067 as possible merge (same hazard, different pipeline stage). Medium confidence - retain both.
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes includes a quality check step. This step may wrongly remove a real clinical finding from the notes. It may also add a finding that the notes do not actually support. This can happen when the AI misreads the instruction it is given.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A genuine disorder or finding is removed by the quality check, or an unsupported finding is added. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible may also link a finding to the wrong part of the body. The altered set of findings then moves forward in the AI workflow. This results in clinical codes being missed or wrong codes being saved into the patient record and into the examples used to teach the AI.
update_risk.harm_description: Clinical coding becomes less accurate. The review queue shown to clinicians may contain missing or incorrect findings. This delays correction and leaves errors in the data used for patient care and clinical reporting.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The AI follows a fixed set of clinical rules when pulling information from notes, which limits the findings it can produce to recognised clinical concepts (DI-3EA60D5A). The AI preserves specific clinical detail, such as how a finding is described, so that the correct clinical code can be assigned (DI-6A0B55A4). All AI-suggested findings go into a single review queue where a trained reviewer checks and corrects them; corrections are saved as structured examples for future AI improvement (DI-890BE989). A reviewer must actively engage with the evidence in the notes before confirming any AI suggestion, and urgency criteria must be met before confirmation is allowed (DI-A23D11FA). If a reviewer corrects a suggestion, the confirmation is reset and the reviewer must re-engage before confirming again (DI-5ADEC3D1). Only authorised staff can review and finalise AI output, enforced by access controls (DI-RBAC enforcement for all AI output review and finalisation actions, DI-E83828A9). Coding corrections are checked against related findings and clinical terminology rules before they are saved (DI-1B8AC856). Quality checks run continuously on clinical coding accuracy, and the system raises an alert if accuracy drops (DI-1126FFD1). The AI model for linking findings to body sites must pass defined quality checks before it is used in live care (DI-80BD2F86). Reviewer engagement is logged and the clinical safety officer monitors this data to detect over-reliance on AI suggestions (DI-22D862B0). The clinical safety committee reviews these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: AI quality check wrongly removes correct clinical codes or sends too many for manual review
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk | Workshop flag: Dedup Auditor flagged R-068 and R-067 as possible merge (same hazard, different pipeline stage). Medium confidence - retain both.
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that checks coding quality may remove clinical codes that are actually correct. It may also flag far too many codes for a clinician to check manually. Both problems can mean that valid clinical codes are never saved to the patient record, or are saved much later than they should be.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: After the AI workflow assigns clinical codes, a second AI quality check runs. This check may wrongly discard a correct code or send it for manual review when it does not need one. If this happens repeatedly, a backlog builds up. In some cases, a code that has been flagged as needing review may still be saved automatically to the patient record without a clinician checking it first.
update_risk.harm_description: Correct and clinically important codes may be missing from the patient record, or may arrive there too late. This can make audit reports and care pathway checks incomplete or misleading. A clinician relying on those reports may not get a full picture of the patient's conditions.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the AI workflow automatically checks the examples used to teach the AI quality checker. It flags any that look wrong and limits how many it can fix on its own. A member of the clinical informatics team reviews the rest. This runs continuously and is reviewed at least monthly (DI-CFA65509). Second, when a code is queried by the quality check, a separate review step checks whether the code is correct and whether it links properly to other codes and clinical terms. A trained coder or clinician carries out this review before any change is saved to the patient record (DI-1B8AC856). Third, the audit programme is set up using real data patterns so that the quality check is calibrated to the actual volume and type of codes seen in practice. The clinical informatics team configures this before any new version is deployed (DI-CD931485). Fourth, every output shown to a clinician includes a clear indicator of how complete and reliable the coding data is. This means a clinician can see at a glance if something may be missing or unverified (DI-900CB621). Fifth, every clinical statement in the system carries a clear link back to the original consultation note and the source code, so a clinician or auditor can trace exactly where each code came from (DI-740BE510). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

add_fmea_item.failure_mode: ConText double-negation inverts assertion on pre-negated SNOMED situation concepts
add_fmea_item.failure_effect: A clinician documents a negative mental health risk screen using a Read or SNOMED situation code whose preferred term begins with "No" (e.g. 134420004 "No suicidal thoughts", 401228008 "No thoughts of deliberate self harm"). The pipeline extracts the span, ConText detects the preceding "No" as a negation cue and sets assertion=absent. The SNOMED concept is then resolved. The persisted coded record now carries assertion=absent on a concept that already means absent -- sema
add_fmea_item.failure_cause: ConText assigns assertion=absent to a SNOMED situation concept whose preferred term already encodes a negative (e.g. "No suicidal thoughts", "No thoughts of deliberate self harm"), inverting the clinical meaning.
add_fmea_item.current_controls: Mitigating DIs: DI-LEO-AI-005, DI-LEO-AI-101, DI-LEO-AI-103, DI-LEO-AI-104
add_fmea_item.recommended_actions: Maintain existing controls and review at quarterly Clinical Safety Committee.

update_risk.title: AI tool misreads 'No suicidal thoughts' and records the opposite meaning
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk | MERGED_IN: R-LEO-AI-071 (ConText double-negation inverts assertion on polarity-encoding SNOMED finding co) per Dedup Auditor
update_risk.hazard_description: Some clinical codes already contain a negative in their name, for example 'No suicidal thoughts' or 'No thoughts of deliberate self-harm'. The AI tool that decides if something is present or absent sees the word 'No' and treats it as a second negation. This flips the meaning, so the record suggests the risk is present when the clinician documented that it is absent.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician completes a mental health risk screen and records a negative finding using a clinical code whose name starts with 'No', such as 'No suicidal thoughts'. The AI workflow pulls this from the notes and the AI tool that decides if something is present or absent detects the word 'No' as a negation signal. It marks the finding as absent. Because the clinical code already means absent, the double negation inverts the intended meaning. The patient record is then saved with a coded entry that implies active suicidal or self-harm ideation, which is the opposite of what the clinician documented.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient record incorrectly suggests the patient has active suicidal ideation or active thoughts of self-harm. A clinician or another system reviewing the record could wrongly escalate the patient's risk level. Alternatively, the documented evidence that the clinician checked and found no risk may be lost. Either outcome could lead to the patient receiving the wrong level of care.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the AI workflow uses a classification step that recognises overlapping and pre-negated clinical codes and handles them separately from ordinary negation cues. This runs automatically every time the AI workflow processes a note (DI-DC61F5B6). Second, the AI tool rates its own confidence for each finding it identifies and flags low-confidence results for human review. This runs automatically on every entry the AI produces (DI-48AD06E5). Third, the coding review card shown to the clinician displays the exact words from the note that led to the present-or-absent decision, so the clinician can spot errors before saving (DI-375C7EB1). Fourth, the text evidence behind each present-or-absent decision is stored alongside the coded entry in the patient record, giving reviewers a clear audit trail (DI-23822663). Fifth, the system component that supplies clinical codes is kept up to date so that pre-negated code names are correctly identified (DI-553F50A2). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and coding accuracy reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working.
