add_fmea_item.failure_mode: Coded entities with absent assertion included in CCI score or cohort selection
add_fmea_item.failure_effect: A patient has an encounter documented with "No diabetes mellitus" coded as a SNOMED finding with assertion='absent'. The CCI query returns this concept because it does not check the assertion field, scoring the patient as diabetic and inflating their comorbidity index. Similarly, cohort filters include the patient in a diabetic cohort they do not belong to.
add_fmea_item.failure_cause: Analytics queries traverse :DOCUMENTS relationships without filtering by assertion status, causing explicitly negated conditions (assertion='absent') to be treated identically to confirmed conditions (assertion='present').
add_fmea_item.recommended_actions: Maintain existing controls and review at quarterly Clinical Safety Committee.

update_risk.title: A condition recorded as absent is wrongly counted as present in a patient's risk score or care group
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible labels some conditions as 'absent' in the notes. However, the system does not check this label when it calculates a patient's comorbidity score or assigns them to a care group. It treats 'absent' conditions the same as confirmed ones.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician documents 'No diabetes' in a patient's notes. The AI tool correctly marks this as absent. But when the system calculates the patient's comorbidity score, it ignores the absent label and counts the diabetes as confirmed. The system gives the patient a higher risk score than they deserve and places them in a diabetes care group they do not belong to.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient receives an incorrect risk score. This can lead to wrong clinical decisions. The patient may get screening invitations they do not need. They may be given the wrong triage priority. Audit reports may show a false picture of the population's health, hiding real problems.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The system checks that the AI tool reading the notes and the AI tool deciding if a condition is present or absent agree on the status of every condition before saving it to the record. This check runs automatically every time notes are processed (DI-F298AE65). Each condition in the record is stored with a clear status: confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive. The system only counts confirmed conditions when calculating scores or assigning care groups. The clinical informatics team sets and maintains these status rules (DI-37DDAADE). The referral triage view applies eligibility rules that require a confirmed condition status before a patient is included in a care group or pathway. This stops patients with absent conditions from being wrongly routed. The clinical team reviews these rules when the system is updated (DI-6C5D77CA). The system suppresses alerts and actions automatically if a coded clinical response confirms a condition is not present. This acts as a safety net if an incorrect score has already been generated. The clinical safety team monitors this function continuously (DI-0E215ADE). Escalation thresholds for investigations are set against comparable groups of patients with confirmed conditions, so a wrongly scored patient would stand out as an outlier. The clinical safety team reviews these thresholds regularly (DI-49A8F570). The clinical safety committee reviews all these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

add_fmea_item.failure_effect: A clinical informatician curates GoldLabel records and edits the source text, leaving entity start/end offsets pointing to wrong characters. Separately, entities with assertion=negated are left in the dataset. If these reach DocBin creation uncorrected, the trained model learns incorrect span boundaries or learns to identify conditions t

update_risk.title: Errors in the examples used to teach the AI cause it to suggest wrong clinical codes
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI learns to recognise conditions in patient notes by studying checked examples. Two faults can corrupt these examples. First, if a clinician edits the source text after marking it up, the marked positions can shift and point to the wrong words. Second, if examples showing that a condition is absent or not confirmed are left in the teaching set by mistake, the AI learns to treat absent conditions as present. Both faults can reach the AI training process uncorrected.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinical informatician reviews and edits patient notes used to teach the AI. After editing, the position markers for clinical terms can drift and point to the wrong characters. Separately, examples where a condition was recorded as absent, not confirmed, or belonging to a family member are not removed before training begins. Both types of faulty example are included in the next AI training run. The AI then learns incorrect boundaries for clinical terms and may treat conditions the patient does not have as if they are present, or miss conditions that are genuinely present.
update_risk.harm_description: The AI suggests wrong clinical codes to clinical staff. Conditions the patient does not have may appear as present diagnoses. Conditions the patient does have may be missed. This can lead to incorrect disease registers, missed Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF) coding, and inaccurate clinical summaries seen by doctors and nurses caring for the patient.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, every clinical term pulled from a patient note is stored with a permanent, unbreakable link back to the exact source text it came from, so any drift in position can be detected before training begins; the engineering team applies this automatically every time examples are prepared (DI-B2512CB3). Second, when a reviewer selects a clinical term to mark up, the tool highlights the exact words in the source note so the reviewer can immediately see if the position is wrong; reviewers use this check during every curation session (DI-E81545BE). Third, when the AI pulls a clinical term from a note it records a confidence score and full details of where the term came from; the clinical safety team inspects these records to spot patterns of error before any training run is approved (DI-31126C6C). Fourth, the process that converts checked examples into the training format preserves every label without loss, so faults are not introduced at the final export step; the engineering team validates this at each export (DI-6EFD68D0). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs from all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended. Additional controls are being identified.

add_fmea_item.failure_mode: NER model assigns spurious additional semantic label to a span, producing an incorrect SNOMED coding in the patient record
add_fmea_item.failure_effect: A GP consultation note is processed by the spancat NER model. The model assigns two semantic labels to a span (e.g. "metformin 500mg" tagged as both substance and procedure). The second label is incorrect. Both labels flow through post-processing and SNOMED resolution, producing two DOCUMENTS relationships on the encounter node: one correct, one spurious. The spurious coding appears in QOF reports, disease prevalence dashboards, or care-pathway episode detection, potentia
add_fmea_item.failure_cause: A spancat NER model trained on multi-label gold data may learn to assign additional semantic labels to spans where only a single label is clinically correct. Unlike the single-label NER, the model can now emit multiple labels per span without an architectural constraint preventing it from doing so.
add_fmea_item.recommended_actions: Additional controls required: DI for spurious-additional-label detector at inference

update_risk.title: The AI tool incorrectly labels clinical information, adding a wrong clinical code to the patient record
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes can label the same piece of text with more than one clinical meaning. Sometimes it adds a second label that is clinically wrong. For example, it might label a medicine as both a drug and a procedure at the same time. There is no built-in check that stops this from happening.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A GP writes a consultation note. The AI tool reads the note and labels a piece of text, such as a medicine name, with two clinical meanings. One label is correct. The other is wrong. Both labels are saved into the patient record as clinical codes. The wrong code then appears in reports used for QOF (Quality and Outcomes Framework) scoring, disease registers, or care pathway alerts. A clinician reading these reports may not realise one code is wrong.
update_risk.harm_description: The wrong clinical code sits in the patient record. It may make it look as though the patient has a condition they do not have. Staff acting on this information could make incorrect treatment decisions. Disease registers and QOF reports may also show inaccurate figures, affecting care planning for wider patient groups.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Five controls are in place to reduce this risk. First, the AI tool is taught using carefully prepared examples that correctly show when more than one label is appropriate; this helps it learn the right boundaries from the start (DI-6EFD68D0). The clinical informatics team maintains these teaching examples and reviews them whenever the AI model is retrained. Second, the AI tool is only allowed to choose labels from a fixed, approved list; it cannot invent new label types outside that list (DI-C899D282). The clinical safety team sets and reviews this approved list at each model release. Third, when the AI tool returns its results, the system checks that each result follows a strict format, one result per label per piece of text; results that do not match this format are rejected before they reach the patient record (DI-6E6C9336). This check runs automatically every time the system processes a note. Fourth, where a piece of text genuinely does carry more than one correct clinical meaning, the system is designed to handle this safely so that only valid combinations are accepted (DI-DC61F5B6). The clinical informatics team reviews these rules at each model update. Fifth, when results are saved into the patient record, the system preserves only the labels that have been correctly matched to a clinical code; unmatched or duplicate labels are flagged and not saved (DI-378F987A). This runs automatically on every record update. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of rejected and flagged labels every quarter to confirm all five controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: Missing or wrong links between clinical findings lead to incorrect coding suggestions
update_risk.description: Source: YAML+FMEA. FMEA refs: FMEA-014. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Consolidates FMEA: FMEA-014
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads notes can attach negation or context to the wrong clinical finding. This happens when the link between two related findings is missing or uses an unsupported type. The result is that the AI misreads what the notes actually say.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A reviewer connects a finding to an unsupported target, or a link between related findings is not saved correctly. The AI workflow then treats those findings as separate, unrelated facts. It suggests an incorrect clinical code based on that misreading.
update_risk.harm_description: An incorrect clinical code can place a patient on the wrong care pathway. It can also distort disease reporting and mislead the reviewing clinician. This may delay recognition of a serious clinical condition.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The AI follows a strict set of rules that only allows supported, valid links between clinical findings. This stops unsupported connections from being made in the first place (DI-3EA60D5A). The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible is limited to working only with structured, confirmed facts from the notes. It cannot draw on information outside those facts (DI-69C29EEF). Every clinical statement carries a record of where it came from and which clinical code it is linked to. This lets reviewers trace any suggestion back to its source (DI-740BE510). The system classifies overlapping clinical findings separately, so one finding does not incorrectly absorb the meaning of another (DI-DC61F5B6). When a reviewer selects a finding, the system highlights the exact words in the original notes that the AI used. The reviewer can then check the AI has read the context correctly (DI-E81545BE). The system compares results against reference ranges and assigns a severity band, flagging findings that may need urgent attention (DI-21E93377). Alerts are automatically suppressed once a clinician has confirmed a coded response, reducing noise for the reviewer (DI-0E215ADE). Every action a clinician takes is saved with their identity and a timestamp. This record cannot be altered (DI-B46AD5CE). Reviewers can filter their worklist by severity, how long a finding has been outstanding, and patient group. This helps them prioritise the most important cases (DI-520A8674). The system maintains a worklist of findings that have not yet been followed up, within a time window that can be adjusted for local needs (DI-4C73DC01). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and worklist data every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: Analysis of too few patients produces misleading results that a clinician acts on
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The tool analyses patient data to find patterns and group patients into pathways. If the underlying data is incomplete or covers too few patients, the results can look reliable but are not. A clinician or service lead may then make a care or pathway decision based on figures that do not reflect reality.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician or service lead runs a pathway analysis on a small group of patients, for example fewer than 30 patients over three months. The tool returns a clear, confident-sounding result. No warning appears to say the data is too thin to trust. The user redesigns a service or changes how patients are triaged based on this result.
update_risk.harm_description: A service change or patient routing decision is made on unreliable evidence. This could delay care, send patients down the wrong pathway, or cause harm by deprioritising patients who need urgent attention.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA).
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The tool shows a data coverage indicator in the research workspace whenever results are based on limited data. This warns the user before they act on the findings (DI-93162C3C). The AI workflow automatically detects gaps in the data and must display a clear warning on any clinician-facing result that is based on incomplete information. This runs every time a result is produced (DI-88F20177). Every clinician-facing output includes a prominent indicator showing how complete and reliable the underlying data is. The clinical team reviews this indicator as part of normal use (DI-900CB621). Each output also shows details about the patient group it is based on, including how many patients were included and over what time period. update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the system keeps an open worklist of findings that have been flagged but not yet acted on, with a configurable time window for follow-up. This gives care coordinators a safety net to catch outstanding results. The clinical team reviews this worklist daily (DI-4C73DC01). Second, every action a clinician takes on a flagged finding is recorded permanently with the clinician's name and the date and time. This creates an auditable trail so nothing can be silently lost. The clinical safety team reviews these records at each audit cycle (DI-B46AD5CE). Third, once a clinician records a confirmed coded clinical response to a finding, the system automatically suppresses duplicate alerts for that finding. This keeps the worklist focused on genuinely unactioned results and reduces the chance that a real gap is hidden by noise (DI-0E215ADE). Fourth, any changes to how the AI workflow is configured can only be made through the user interface, and a separate approval step is required before a failed test mode can be promoted to live use. This stops untested configuration changes from silently worsening the problem (DI-F2C18D2E). The clinical safety committee reviews all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: AI tool wrongly labels a diagnosis appointment as a referral, making the wait time look near-zero
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: Some appointment notes mention fast-track or two-week-wait (2WW) referrals in passing. The AI tool that reads notes can mistake this mention for a new referral happening on that same day. When this happens, the system treats the diagnosis appointment date as the referral date. This wipes out the real, earlier referral that was already recorded.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A quality-improvement lead opens the Diagnostic Interval dashboard. They see a group of patients whose time from referral to diagnosis looks almost zero. They may wrongly conclude the pathway is performing well and miss a real delay earlier in the process. Or they may distrust the data entirely and go back to checking records by hand.
update_risk.harm_description: The quality-improvement lead acts on wrong information. Pathway delays go unnoticed and unaddressed. Conversion-rate figures look better than they really are. Clinicians and managers lose trust in the analytics tool.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool scores its own confidence each time it pulls information from a note, including when it identifies a referral (DI-48AD06E5). This score is recorded alongside every referral it finds, so low-confidence findings can be spotted. The AI workflow applies this check automatically every time a note is processed. Second, an episode quality gate blocks any episode with unresolved warning flags from appearing in reports (DI-A0579B64). This means a wrongly dated episode cannot reach the dashboard until a clinician or analyst has reviewed and cleared the flag. The system applies this gate continuously before any data is published. Third, the pathway timeline view highlights unusual gaps or near-zero intervals so that reviewers can see at a glance when something looks wrong (DI-4885D9FF). Analysts use this view during routine dashboard checks. Fourth, the clinic list preparation view shows pathway status alongside comparator data, making it easier to spot episodes that look out of step with similar patients (DI-CF03E4EA). Clinicians and quality leads use this view when preparing for clinics and review meetings. Fifth, automated coding quality checks run continuously and raise an alert if accuracy drops or a pattern of errors appears (DI-1126FFD1). The clinical informatics team reviews these alerts and acts on any regression. The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk

It does not check which cancer pathway each note belongs to. This means staging details — such as TNM stage or Gleason score — from one cancer can be wrongly linked to a different cancer on the same patient.

It uses the staging details from that letter to record the stage for the bowel cancer episode instead. The bowel cancer stage saved in the system is clinically wrong. The cancer tracker and national audit submissions then show the wrong stage for that patient.

update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)

update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. Second, an automatic quality gate blocks any episode with a flagged problem from being included in reports or audit submissions until a clinician has reviewed and resolved the flag (DI-A0579B64). This runs continuously for every episode and is monitored by the clinical safety committee monthly. Third, the cohort builder applies rule-based filters — including cancer pathway type — so that only notes belonging to the correct pathway are used when building each patient episode (DI-FE3FFE50). The informatics team reviews these filter rules at each software release. Fourth, the MDT case summary template includes a pathway checklist that prompts the reviewing clinician to confirm that staging details match the correct cancer site before sign-off (DI-DBC2399F). update_risk.title: Safety-net alerts are generated but not shown on the worklist, or marking an alert as actioned appears to work but saves nothing
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The system detects that a patient needs safety-netting follow-up but fails to save the alert. Separately, when a clinician marks an alert as actioned, the system confirms success but does not actually update the record. This can happen because the AI workflow looks up the wrong identifier when saving changes back into the patient record.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A GP or nurse opens the safety-netting worklist and sees no alerts, even though the system has detected that a patient is missing safety-netting advice or has been waiting too long for a referral. Or the clinician clicks 'mark actioned', the screen shows success, but the alert remains open in the background. No escalation is triggered. The patient's at-risk status is never reviewed.
update_risk.harm_description: The clinician does not know the patient needs follow-up. The patient misses a timely review. This can delay diagnosis in cancer or other time-critical pathways, causing serious harm.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the system maintains a worklist of all outstanding safety-net alerts within a set follow-up time window. This gives clinicians a visible list of patients who still need action. The system runs this continuously and the clinical team reviews the worklist at every clinical session (DI-4C73DC01). Second, the system automatically removes an alert from the worklist only when a confirmed clinical response has been recorded in the patient record. This stops alerts from disappearing without a real clinical action. The system applies this check every time a record is updated (DI-0E215ADE). Third, the worklist can be filtered by how serious the alert is, how many days it has been outstanding, and which group of patients it covers. This helps clinicians spot the most urgent cases quickly. Clinicians apply these filters during their worklist review (DI-520A8674). Fourth, every time a clinician actions an alert, the system saves an unchangeable record of who did it and when. This means any silent failure to save would be visible as a missing record. The system creates this record at the point of action and the safety team audits it regularly (DI-B46AD5CE). Fifth, if a quality check detects that alerts are not being acknowledged at the expected rate, the system raises an escalation alert and automatically pauses the AI workflow until the problem is investigated. The system monitors this threshold continuously and the clinical safety committee reviews any pauses promptly (DI-5A802C83). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: A staff member misunderstands on-screen guidance and approves the wrong AI rule, causing incorrect quality reporting figures
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: adequate. Existing YAML risk | Workshop flag: Dedup Auditor flagged R-094 health-literacy overlap with R-081. Medium confidence - retain both.
update_risk.hazard_description: The system shows each user a short introduction card when they open the rules management screen. If that card is wrong, missing, or uses technical language the user cannot understand, the user may take the wrong action. For example, they might approve a rule they do not understand or delete a rule that is still needed.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A junior coding clerk opens the rules management screen. The introduction card uses technical language about how the AI tool decides whether a condition is present or absent. The clerk does not understand the card but ticks 'approve' anyway. The approved rule then causes the AI tool to incorrectly record conditions as absent when they are present. This feeds wrong figures into the Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF) report for that period.
update_risk.harm_description: QOF report figures are wrong for the affected reporting period. The error is not caught until a later quality check. No patient's clinical record is changed without a clinician reviewing it first, so there is no direct harm to any individual patient. However, the practice may lose confidence in the accuracy of its audit reports.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA).
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the system shows the reviewer the AI tool's decision alongside the supporting evidence from the patient notes, so the reviewer can see why the AI reached its conclusion before approving anything. This is built into the coding review screen and is available every time a reviewer uses it (DI-375C7EB1). Second, the rules management workspace uses plain English throughout, so staff without a technical background can understand what they are being asked to do. The development team maintains this at every release (DI-DD67ACFF). Third, the system shows plain-English summaries of what each coded finding means, so reviewers are not relying on clinical codes alone. This is available to all reviewers at all times (DI-66F1B177). Fourth, before any rule change is saved, the system runs a report showing how that change would affect a sample of existing patient records. This gives the reviewer a clear picture of the impact before they confirm the change. The system runs this check automatically every time a rule is edited (DI-48C13EB6). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and reviewer feedback every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The system merges tasks from three separate sources into one list, sorted by urgency. Tasks from one source can slip to the bottom of the list if other tasks look more urgent by their urgency band. A member of staff who only checks the first page may not notice that, for example, the number of safety-net alerts has doubled overnight.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A safety-net alert sits unactioned past its deadline because the combined list has pushed it below coding-review tasks. Those coding tasks appear more urgent by their urgency band, but the safety-net alert is clinically more pressing.
update_risk.harm_description: If a safety-net alert is not acted on in time, a patient may not receive a follow-up they need. The risk is limited because safety-net alerts have their own separate escalation route outside this list. This is a risk about how easy the screen is to use, not a risk of losing patient data.

update_risk.title: The dashboard undercounts cancer diagnoses that came through the two-week-wait (2WW) referral route, making the figure look far lower than it should be
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: The tool that builds cancer episodes has two faults. First, it rejects referrals where the cancer site is not clearly recorded, so most episodes are left without a linked referral. Second, when no referral is linked, the tool fills the referral date with the diagnosis date instead. Together, these faults mean the dashboard shows only around 18% of cancer diagnoses as coming via the 2WW route. The true national figure is 50 to 60%. The gap is caused by a flaw in how the tool matches referrals to diagnoses, not by a real problem in the practice.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A practice quality lead looks at the dashboard and sees that only 18% of cancer diagnoses came via the 2WW route. This is far below the expected 50 to 60%. They do not know the figure is wrong. They may start an improvement programme to fix a problem that does not exist at that scale. They may report the false figure to their ICB, CCG, or Royal College. When they later discover the numbers are inaccurate, they may lose confidence in the whole tool.
update_risk.harm_description: Clinical improvement effort is wasted on a problem that is not real. False figures may be reported to national bodies. The tool is designed to act as a safety net for cancer pathways. This fault corrupts that safety-net signal. There is no direct harm to an individual patient, but the reliability of the tool as a whole is undermined.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Five controls are in place to reduce this risk. First, the episode quality gate blocks any episode marked with a quality flag from appearing in reports until the flag is resolved. This stops flawed data reaching clinicians. The system runs this check automatically every time an episode is processed (DI-A0579B64). Second, the dashboard shows national benchmark figures alongside local figures. A clinician can immediately see when a local figure is far outside the expected range. The system displays this comparison continuously (DI-BA2C8F3E). Third, the safety-netting alert system automatically suppresses an alert once a confirmed clinical response has been recorded in the patient record. This prevents the same gap from triggering repeated false alarms (DI-0E215ADE). Fourth, the worklist filter lets a quality lead sort and review outstanding alerts by how serious they are, how long they have been open, and which group of patients they affect. This helps the team spot patterns that suggest a data quality problem rather than a real clinical gap. The quality lead uses this filter as part of routine review (DI-520A8674). Fifth, the audit quality loop records the root cause of every drift alert and keeps an unchangeable two-year history of all alerts. This lets the safety team trace when the undercounting started and confirm when it has been fixed. The team reviews this log as part of ongoing monitoring (DI-B1E0EE52). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: The AI tool that merges duplicate episodes could wrongly combine two separate primary cancers into one record
update_risk.description: Source: YAML. FMEA refs: n/a. Workshop decision: confirm. Control adequacy: partial. Existing YAML risk
update_risk.hazard_description: A patient can have two genuinely different primary cancers diagnosed close together in time. For example, a breast cancer found at mammography and a melanoma (skin cancer) found at a dermatology review 30 days later. The AI workflow uses a 180-day window to decide whether two episodes are the same event. If both cancers fall inside that window, the AI may treat them as one episode and hide the second cancer behind a merged flag.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviewing the patient record for audit sees only the breast cancer episode. The melanoma episode is hidden because the AI has merged it into the first. The melanoma pathway, including its stage, treatment start, and any safety-netting alerts, is no longer visible in the main audit view. If the clinician does not look for merged records, the melanoma is effectively invisible during the audit.
update_risk.harm_description: The audit fails to detect the second primary cancer. The patient's underlying clinical record is still intact, so there is no direct harm to the patient at the point of care. However, the melanoma is missing from the audit workflow. This means multi-primary cancer patients may be under-reported and any safety-netting signals for the melanoma may be missed by the audit team.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the AI workflow builds each episode from related clinical encounters using fixed, predictable rules rather than guesswork, which reduces the chance of a wrong merge in the first place (DI-FF9C74E2). This runs automatically each time the system processes new encounter data. Second, a human-review gate stops any unreviewed episode classification from being used in audit reports (DI-BD696225). A trained reviewer must approve each episode before it appears in audit outputs. This check runs before every audit report is generated. Third, the safety-netting worklist lets clinicians filter outstanding alerts by how serious they are, how long they have been open, and which patient group they affect (DI-520A8674). The clinical team reviews this worklist regularly to catch any cancer pathway signals that have not been acted on. Fourth, the AI tool automatically suppresses a safety-netting alert only when a confirmed clinical response has been coded in the record (DI-0E215ADE). This prevents alerts from being silently closed without a clinician having responded. Fifth, the AI tool produces a structured summary of coded encounters, pathway stage, and safety-netting alerts for each patient (DI-30D9CC61). Reviewers can use this summary to spot gaps, such as a missing second cancer pathway, before the audit is finalised. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and worklist completion rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: Patient missed by the system and not invited to the programme
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-004. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: adequate. No risk on shortlisting false negatives - create R-LEO-AI-078
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads clinical notes may fail to recognise a relevant encounter. Separately, the system may fail to build a complete clinical episode from those encounters. Either failure can mean the system does not flag the patient for the programme.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient who should be invited to the programme is not identified. The system does not add them to the shortlist. No clinician is alerted. The patient receives no invitation and misses the care pathway.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient does not receive timely assessment or treatment through the programme. A serious or worsening condition may go undetected. This could lead to significant harm, including delayed diagnosis or avoidable deterioration.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system must correctly identify at least 95 in every 100 eligible patients when tested against cases checked by an expert. The AI tool cannot go live unless it meets this accuracy threshold. The clinical safety team checks this before every release (DI-10BB41E9). Second, the system uses three different methods to search for relevant encounters: keyword search, full-text search, and meaning-based search. Using all three together reduces the chance of missing a patient. The technical team configures and maintains these search methods (DI-143F69EB). Third, each patient the system shortlists is given a ranked relevance score with supporting evidence from the notes. Clinicians can see why a patient was included or excluded. This is reviewed during clinical audit (DI-4746A178). Fourth, every episode is labelled as confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive. This makes it clear when the system is uncertain, so a clinician can review borderline cases. The clinical team reviews inconclusive cases as part of routine workflow (DI-37DDAADE). Fifth, the system must reach at least 85% accuracy when classifying episodes, measured against cases agreed by expert clinicians. The system cannot be deployed unless it meets this standard. The clinical safety team checks this at each release (DI-736B698B). Sixth, the rules the system uses to decide who is eligible are stored separately from the software code and are version-controlled. Changes to eligibility criteria can be made without a software release, and every change is recorded. The programme lead reviews and approves any changes (DI-1501326A). Seventh, any encounter the system fails to process is listed automatically, with the reason for failure shown. A member of the operations team can requeue failed encounters with a single action. The operations team reviews this list daily (DI-69CE20C1). Eighth, the AI workflow that classifies encounters uses managed rules, records its decision for each encounter, and must pass a test before any rule change takes effect. The technical team runs these tests before every update (DI-8CE01B3E). Ninth, any change to the system is risk-scored before it reaches live patients. High-risk changes are blocked from deployment until approved. The clinical safety officer reviews and approves high-risk changes (DI-7C5EC850). Tenth, all patient record data flows through a standard health data interface, and every audit result is exported through the same interface. This ensures data is not lost or corrupted in transit. The technical team monitors this continuously (DI-1795254D). Eleventh, the system processes each patient's full record within 10 seconds for 95 in every 100 patients. Slow processing is flagged automatically so delays do not cause patients to be missed. The technical team monitors processing times daily (DI-620FE631). The clinical safety committee reviews all these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

update_risk.title: A patient is wrongly added to a care pathway (false positive)
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-005. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: adequate. Lower severity but high volume effect - create R-LEO-AI-079
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads clinical notes uses rules that are too broad. It may flag a patient as needing review when they do not. This can happen when the rules do not distinguish clearly enough between patients who meet the criteria and those who do not.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient who does not meet the programme criteria is placed on the review worklist. A clinician may then spend time reviewing that patient unnecessarily. In some cases, the clinician may act on the incorrect inclusion and offer the patient an intervention they do not need.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient may receive unnecessary clinical contact, investigation, or treatment. This causes minor harm, including avoidable anxiety or inconvenience. It also uses clinical time that could be spent on patients who genuinely need review.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system must correctly identify at least 95% of patients who truly meet the criteria, using a set of records checked by a clinical expert. This accuracy check is run by the development team before each release and after any change to the AI tool (DI-10BB41E9). Second, the inclusion criteria for the programme are stored as a versioned configuration file. The clinical team can update the criteria without changing the underlying software, reducing the risk of overly broad rules persisting unnoticed (DI-1501326A). Third, the AI tool uses three different methods to search clinical records, including keyword search, full-text search, and meaning-based search. Results from all three are combined and ranked by relevance. This helps the system avoid flagging patients based on a single weak signal (DI-143F69EB, DI-4746A178). Fourth, the worklist shows the clinician the supporting evidence from the patient record that led to the inclusion. The clinician can see at a glance why the patient was flagged and can quickly spot an error (DI-4746A178). Fifth, the system tells the reviewer whether each patient was classified by a fixed rule or by the AI tool acting as a fallback. This helps the clinician judge how much confidence to place in the result (DI-8C236A1A). Sixth, the worklist can be filtered by severity and patient group, so clinicians can prioritise genuine cases and are less likely to act on a false positive without scrutiny (DI-520A8674). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data on false positive rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working. Additional controls are being identified.

update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient has a condition that should be tracked as a care episode. The system does not create the episode because it did not pick up the relevant clinical code. The condition is not added to the patient's episode list. The clinician sees an incomplete picture of the patient's care history.
update_risk.harm_description: The clinician does not see the full care history for the patient. They may miss that a condition is present or that a care pathway has not been completed. This could lead to a delayed diagnosis, a missed treatment step, or an unsafe clinical decision. The patient could come to serious harm as a result.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system is built so that episodes are always constructed from linked clinical encounters using fixed, predictable rules rather than guesswork. This means a missing code is less likely to cause a silent gap (DI-FF9C74E2). The system runs automatic checks on every episode to spot unusual durations, missing care milestones, and steps that appear in the wrong order. These checks run each time the AI workflow processes a patient record (DI-1206D9E8). Every episode is given a clear status of confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive so reviewers can see at a glance which episodes need attention (DI-37DDAADE). The system shows the reviewer a plain-English summary of the clinical codes it found, so they can spot if something important has been missed (DI-66F1B177). The system also tells the reviewer whether each episode was created by fixed rules or by the AI tool that reads notes, so they know how much to trust the result (DI-8C236A1A). No episode classification can be used in audit reports until a clinician has reviewed and approved it. This human-review step acts as a safety net before any output reaches decision-makers (DI-BD696225). The AI tool that reads notes must reach at least 85 per cent accuracy against examples checked by an expert before it is used in live care. The clinical safety team checks this accuracy score before each new version is released (DI-736B698B). The episode timeline view highlights any gaps in the expected care pathway so the reviewing clinician can see where something may have been missed (DI-4885D9FF). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and accuracy reports every quarter to confirm all these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: The system removes too much clinical detail when hiding patient identifiers
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-013. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: partial. Over-redaction not covered - create R-LEO-AI-082
update_risk.hazard_description: Before sending notes to the AI, the system hides patient identifiers such as dates, ages, and locations. If the system removes too much, important clinical details may be lost. For example, a patient's age or the date of a key event may be stripped out along with the identifier. The AI then works on incomplete information.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviews the AI output, which is based on notes with missing clinical details. The clinician may not realise that dates, ages, or location-related clinical facts were removed. They may act on an incomplete picture of the patient's history.
update_risk.harm_description: The clinician makes a clinical decision based on incomplete information. For example, a time-sensitive diagnosis or an age-dependent medicine dose could be missed or miscalculated. This could lead to a delayed or incorrect treatment decision, causing minor harm to the patient.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system uses reversible placeholder substitution when hiding patient identifiers. This means identifiers are replaced with temporary labels, not deleted, so clinical meaning is preserved. The original details are held securely in memory for the session only and never shared with the AI. The software engineering team builds and maintains this control (DI-250F32EC). Second, a mandatory safety check runs automatically before any notes reach the AI. This check cannot be switched off or bypassed. It confirms that the hiding process has run correctly before the AI sees any information. The software engineering team maintains this control (DI-F66A7239). Third, the AI is only allowed to interpret facts that are present in the structured input it receives. It cannot fill in gaps or guess missing details. This limits the risk of the AI producing output based on assumed rather than real clinical facts. The clinical informatics team defines and maintains these boundaries (DI-69C29EEF). Fourth, the AI follows a defined set of clinical rules when pulling information from notes. This reduces the chance of clinical relationships being misread or lost during the hiding process (DI-3EA60D5A). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and test results for these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended. Additional controls are being identified.

update_risk.title: Alert incorrectly suppressed because a clinical response code was recorded in error
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-015. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: partial. Incorrect suppression scenario not covered - create R-LEO-AI-083
update_risk.hazard_description: The system can suppress an alert when it believes a clinician has already responded to a finding. If a clinical response code is recorded in error, the system may treat an unreviewed finding as already dealt with. The alert is then hidden, and no further action is prompted.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A patient has an abnormal test result that needs clinical review. A response code is recorded against that result by mistake. The system reads this code and suppresses the alert. The clinician never sees the alert and does not know the result is outstanding. The patient does not receive timely follow-up.
update_risk.harm_description: A serious or life-threatening abnormal result goes unreviewed. The patient does not receive the treatment or follow-up they need. This could lead to significant harm or death, particularly where the result indicates a critical condition.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system only suppresses an alert when a confirmed clinical response code is recorded against the correct result. This is an automated check that runs every time an alert is about to be suppressed (DI-0E215ADE). Second, every action that suppresses an alert is saved permanently with the clinician's identity and the exact date and time. This record cannot be changed or deleted. The clinical team can review it at any time (DI-B46AD5CE). Third, the system compares each result against reference ranges and assigns a severity band. High-severity results are flagged more prominently, making it harder for a suppressed alert to go unnoticed (DI-21E93377). Fourth, a worklist shows all outstanding flagged findings, filtered by severity, how long they have been waiting, and which patient group they belong to. A clinician reviews this worklist regularly to catch any results that should not have been suppressed (DI-520A8674). Fifth, the system uses a configurable follow-up time window. If a flagged finding has not been resolved within that window, it reappears on the worklist. This acts as a safety net if suppression was applied in error (DI-4C73DC01). Sixth, the thresholds that control when suppression is applied are set at programme level by a named administrator. Changes to these thresholds are reviewed and approved before they take effect (DI-0D7DCC52). Seventh, suppression thresholds for normal-range results are also set at programme level and reviewed separately, reducing the risk that suppression rules are applied too broadly (DI-79509E39). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of suppressed alerts and worklist compliance every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

update_risk.title: Wrong reference range applied to a test result
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-017. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: partial. Reference range data quality risk - create R-LEO-AI-085
update_risk.hazard_description: The system stores reference ranges (the normal values used to judge a test result). If a reference range is entered with the wrong numbers or the wrong units, the system will use that wrong range to judge every patient result it checks against it.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviews a test result that the system has flagged as normal. The system has compared the result against a wrong reference range. The result is actually abnormal. The clinician does not realise this and takes no action.
update_risk.harm_description: The clinician misses an abnormal result. The patient does not receive the investigation or treatment they need. Depending on the clinical condition, this could cause serious or life-threatening harm.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, when anyone enters or changes a reference range, the system requires them to record where the range comes from and confirm the units of measure. This stops ranges being saved without a clear source (DI-340279C1). Second, a dashboard shows the review status of every reference range in the system. The clinical team checks this dashboard regularly to spot ranges that are out of date or unreviewed (DI-E7609DD8). Third, any change to a reference range cannot go live until an approval record has been completed. The system blocks activation without this record (DI-C5A523A7). Fourth, when the system checks a result against a reference range, it classifies the result into one of three severity bands and flags anything outside the normal range. This gives the clinician a clear signal if a result is abnormal (DI-21E93377). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and dashboard data every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

update_risk.title: Reference range out of date because a clinical guideline has changed
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-018. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: partial. Reference range staleness risk - create R-LEO-AI-086
update_risk.hazard_description: The system stores reference ranges (the normal values used to judge a test result). When a clinical guideline changes, the system may not prompt anyone to update the stored range. The AI workflow continues to use the old value without warning.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviews a patient's test result. The system compares it against an out-of-date reference range. The result appears normal on screen. In fact, under the current guideline, the result is abnormal and needs action.
update_risk.harm_description: The clinician does not act on an abnormal result because the system showed it as normal. The patient's condition goes unrecognised and untreated. This could cause serious harm, for example a missed diagnosis of a dangerous condition such as kidney disease or anaemia.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, every reference range must be entered with a named source and a unit of measure. This creates a clear record of where each range came from and makes it easier to spot when a source guideline changes (DI-340279C1). The clinical informatics team sets this up when a range is first added. Second, a currency dashboard lists every reference range alongside its review status. The clinical safety team checks this dashboard regularly to find ranges that have not been reviewed recently (DI-E7609DD8). Third, a change control gate stops any updated range from going live until an approval record has been completed. No change can be activated without sign-off (DI-C5A523A7). The clinical safety officer approves each change before it is released. Fourth, a risk-scored change queue holds pending updates in order of clinical importance. A production deployment interlock means no change reaches live systems until the queue item is cleared (DI-7C5EC850). The clinical safety team manages this queue on an ongoing basis. An additional safety net runs automatically each time a result is processed. It compares the result against the current reference range and flags it in one of three severity bands, alerting the clinician if the result falls outside normal limits (DI-21E93377). The clinical safety committee reviews the effectiveness of all five controls every quarter.

update_risk.title: A reference range is changed without proper approval
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-019. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: adequate. Lower probability but regulatory impact - note at workshop
update_risk.hazard_description: The system allows a reference range to be added, edited, or deleted without going through the required approval steps. A reference range tells the system what counts as a normal or abnormal test result. If this changes without approval, the system may use wrong thresholds without anyone knowing.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician or administrator changes a reference range outside the approved process. The system then compares patient test results against the wrong thresholds. Abnormal results may appear normal, or normal results may trigger unnecessary alerts. Clinicians make decisions based on incorrect information.
update_risk.harm_description: A patient with a genuinely abnormal result is not flagged. The clinician does not investigate or treat. The patient comes to serious harm because a critical condition is missed or treated incorrectly.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: First, the system only allows reference ranges to be entered or changed using a structured form that requires a source and a unit of measure to be recorded. This stops incomplete or untraceable changes being saved (DI-340279C1). Second, the system blocks any reference range from becoming active unless an approval record has been completed. No approval means no change goes live (DI-C5A523A7). Third, before any change is approved, the person requesting it must complete a clinical impact assessment explaining how the change could affect patients. This is checked by a senior clinician before sign-off (DI-59F2B21E). Fourth, all reference ranges appear on a content dashboard that shows their review status. The clinical team checks this dashboard to spot ranges that are overdue for review (DI-E7609DD8). Fifth, the system automatically compares every patient result against the current reference range and classifies it into one of three severity bands. This means a wrongly set range is more likely to be noticed quickly because results behave unexpectedly (DI-21E93377). Sixth, any reference range linked to a NICE technology appraisal or quality standard is tracked with a deadline timer so required updates are not missed (DI-44802DF3). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of all reference range changes and checks that every change has a complete approval record every quarter.

update_risk.title: Clinical code saved without a link to its source in the notes
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-021. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: adequate. No explicit provenance loss risk - create R-LEO-AI-087
update_risk.hazard_description: When the AI tool reads a patient's notes and finds a clinical term, it must save a link back to the exact words it used. If that link is not saved, no one can check where the clinical code came from.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviews a coded entry in the patient record, for example a diagnosis of hypertension (high blood pressure). There is no link to the original words in the notes. The clinician cannot tell whether the AI tool read the notes correctly. A wrong or misleading code may go unchallenged and stay in the record.
update_risk.harm_description: A patient's record contains an incorrect clinical code with no way to trace or correct it. Future clinicians rely on that code when making decisions about the patient's care. The patient may receive the wrong treatment, miss a needed referral, or be harmed by a decision based on inaccurate information.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The AI workflow always saves a fixed link between each clinical code and the exact words in the notes it came from. This link cannot be changed or deleted after it is created (DI-B2512CB3). Every clinical statement the system produces must carry both the source encounter and the clinical code together, so the link is never missing from the start (DI-740BE510). The AI tool records the full source text alongside every decision it makes about whether a condition is present, absent, or possible, so reviewers can check its reasoning (DI-23822663). When a clinician reviews a coded entry, the system highlights the original words in the notes that the AI tool used, making it easy to spot errors (DI-E81545BE). The system stores the precise position of each term in the original notes so the highlight always points to the right place (DI-A0C90595). Every clinical code is saved with a confidence score and full source information so reviewers know how certain the AI tool was (DI-31126C6C). The AI tool preserves clinical detail, such as whether a condition is mild or severe, so codes are as specific as possible and less likely to mislead (DI-6A0B55A4). When a reviewer corrects a coded entry, that correction is permanently linked to the original source information and cannot be separated from it (DI-4F67189B). All source links and provenance records are kept for a minimum of seven years and cannot be deleted (DI-080A2454). Authorised staff can look up the full history of any coded entry without accessing the wider patient record (DI-09E26C1D). Any proposed change to the AI workflow that could affect these links is held in a review queue and cannot go live until it has been checked and approved (DI-7C5EC850). Annotators who label examples used to teach the AI are checked for consistency, so the AI learns correct linking behaviour from the start (DI-EE80C271). The clinical safety committee reviews audit reports of provenance completeness every quarter to confirm all controls are working.

update_risk.title: System fails to show the clinician the escalation threshold when reviewing a test result
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-022. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: partial. No risk on guideline threshold surfacing failure - create R-LEO-AI-088
update_risk.hazard_description: The system holds guidelines that tell clinicians when a test result needs urgent action. If a guideline has not been linked to the correct test type, or the threshold value is missing, the system cannot show the warning. The clinician sees the result but gets no prompt that it has crossed a level requiring escalation.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviews an abnormal test result during a routine consultation. The system does not display the relevant guideline threshold because the link between the guideline and the test type is absent or incomplete. The clinician has no prompt to escalate and may assume the result is within acceptable limits.
update_risk.harm_description: The clinician does not escalate the patient in time. A serious condition such as acute kidney injury or a dangerously abnormal blood count goes untreated or is treated too late. The patient suffers avoidable harm, which could include hospital admission, organ damage, or death.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The system shows the clinician the escalation threshold alongside every test result, with a comparison to similar patients on the same care programme. This runs automatically each time a result is reviewed (DI-49A8F570). The system is set up to suppress alerts only for results that are clearly within the normal range. Thresholds for suppression are agreed at programme level by the clinical team and reviewed regularly, so abnormal results always trigger a visible prompt (DI-79509E39). Every panel showing clinical information carries a permanent notice reminding the clinician that the output is a decision-support tool and does not replace clinical judgement. This notice is always visible and cannot be dismissed (DI-E609C4E5). When a clinician orders a test, the system displays the relevant guideline norms and comparator values at the point of ordering, reinforcing awareness of thresholds before results arrive (DI-F235845B). Partial results are shown to the clinician as soon as each step of the AI workflow is complete, rather than waiting for all steps to finish. This means the clinician sees available threshold information sooner (DI-CB07829F). All patient data coming into the system and all audit outputs leaving it follow a recognised clinical data standard, ensuring threshold records are structured consistently and can be checked for completeness (DI-1795254D). The system flags any test result where the displayed information diverges from the current guideline, and records a change history so the clinical team can spot patterns of missing thresholds. The impact review panel highlights these gaps for the clinical team to act on (DI-0C8FBAF7). The clinical safety committee reviews audit reports of threshold coverage and alert suppression settings every quarter to confirm all controls are working as intended.

update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-024. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: partial. Guideline staleness at point of clinical use - create R-LEO-AI-089
update_risk.hazard_description: The system may show a treatment recommendation based on an old clinical guideline. Guidelines change when new evidence emerges. If the system is not updated promptly, it will show advice that no longer reflects current best practice.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician reads the system's treatment suggestion during a consultation. The suggestion is based on a guideline that has since been updated or withdrawn. The clinician does not realise the advice is out of date. They follow it when making a decision about the patient's care.
update_risk.harm_description: The patient receives treatment that is no longer recommended. This could mean they miss a safer or more effective option. In the most serious cases, outdated advice could lead to avoidable harm or a delayed diagnosis.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: A guideline monitoring registry tracks all clinical guidelines the system uses. A named clinician reviews the registry whenever a guideline changes and approves any update before it goes live. This is managed under formal clinical change control, so no update is made without a documented check (DI-ED3A89F5). The system shows each recommendation alongside a summary of the evidence behind it, including how recent that evidence is. This helps the clinician judge whether the advice looks current (DI-82D5359B). A currency dashboard shows the clinical safety team which guidelines are due for review and flags any that may be out of date. The team can export this information for audit (DI-E5609239). The system displays treatment options without ranking them, and tells the clinician which patient group the evidence applies to. This reduces the risk that a clinician follows a single suggestion without thinking critically (DI-76C86329). The system shows a confidence level alongside each piece of AI-generated information, so the clinician can see how certain the system is (DI-DA7584D8). The system does not make final diagnostic or treatment decisions on its own. It supports the clinician, who retains responsibility for the final decision (DI-A3107424). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs from the guideline registry and the currency dashboard every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

update_risk.title: Treatment comparisons based on an unrepresentative group of patients
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-025. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: partial. Comparator bias risk - workshop priority
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool learns from examples of past patients to suggest treatments. If those past patients are not a fair or representative sample, the comparisons the AI offers may not reflect what is likely to happen for the patient in front of the clinician. The AI does not flag when its comparison group is a poor match.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviews the AI's suggested treatment options. The options are ranked using outcome data from a group of patients who do not closely match the current patient. The clinician does not realise the comparison group is unrepresentative. They may favour a treatment that looks better in the data but is not the best choice for this patient.
update_risk.harm_description: The clinician chooses a treatment based on misleading comparisons. The patient receives a treatment that is less effective or less safe than the best available option. This could lead to their condition worsening, a delayed recovery, or an avoidable complication.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the system shows all treatment options in a neutral, unranked list and tells the clinician which group of past patients the comparisons come from, in plain language. This helps the clinician judge whether the comparison group is a good match. The development team sets this up as a design requirement and the clinical safety team checks it works during testing (DI-76C86329). Second, the system displays the relevant clinical guideline recommendation alongside each outcome summary, so the clinician can compare the AI suggestion against established guidance. The development team builds this in and the clinical safety team reviews it during testing (DI-82D5359B). Third, the system shows the clinician exactly which criteria were used to select the comparison group of patients, and asks the clinician to confirm they have noted this before proceeding. Any confirmation is saved in the audit log. This runs automatically every time a treatment suggestion is shown (DI-6079EC71). Fourth, any change to how the AI selects its comparison group must pass a safety review before it goes live. The development team manages this queue and no change can be released without sign-off from the clinical safety team (DI-7C5EC850). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and incident reports related to this risk every quarter to confirm all four controls are working as intended.

Non-blocking investigation deviation acknowledgement with logged rationale and visible cohort match criteria

update_risk.title: Recovery markers missed from the patient's coded record
update_risk.description: Source: FMEA_GAP. FMEA refs: FMEA-026. Workshop decision: adjust. Control adequacy: partial. Create R-LEO-AI-090
update_risk.hazard_description: The AI tool that reads clinical notes may not recognise all the clinical codes that show a patient is recovering. Some recovery markers may fall outside the range of codes the AI tool has been taught to look for. This means the system may not pick up signs that a patient's condition is improving or worsening after treatment.
update_risk.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviews a patient's progress after treatment. The system fails to identify key recovery markers in the patient's record. The clinician sees an incomplete picture of the patient's recovery. They may not realise the patient is deteriorating or that a follow-up is needed.
update_risk.harm_description: The clinician makes a clinical decision based on incomplete information. A patient who is not recovering as expected does not receive timely review or intervention. This could lead to serious harm, including delayed diagnosis of a complication or failure to escalate care.
update_risk.identified_by: LEO-AI-CORE Hazard Workshop 2026-04-16 (facilitated by Rob Smith)
update_risk.monitoring_plan: Monitor via DQ dashboards, incident management, and quarterly RPN trend review at Clinical Safety Committee. Specialist framework: clinical safety.
update_risk.mitigation_measures_detail: The AI workflow uses a classification approach that can handle overlapping clinical codes, reducing the chance that recovery markers are missed (DI-DC61F5B6). This is built into the system design and applies every time the system processes a patient record. The AI tool preserves important clinical detail, such as whether a finding is confirmed, absent, or possible, when pulling information from notes and matching it to clinical codes (DI-6A0B55A4). This runs automatically each time the system reads a clinical entry. The system is taught using examples that have been checked by an expert and kept separate from the data used to test it, so its accuracy on recovery markers can be measured reliably (DI-BB64E479). The clinical safety team reviews this separation before each new version is released. When the system pulls a clinical code from a note, it records how confident it is and where the information came from, so clinicians and reviewers can check its work (DI-31126C6C). This provenance record is available at all times. The system includes post-treatment recovery markers and uses comparable patient journeys to set expectations for recovery (DI-49403C92). Clinicians are alerted when a patient's progress does not match the expected pattern. If the system flags a deviation from the expected recovery path, the clinician must document a structured response rather than simply dismissing the alert (DI-BD826FA6). This applies every time an alert is generated. The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.
